## src/

The app shell: the entry point, the layout, and the problem-report and credits data.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`App.tsx`](../src/App.tsx) | The app's layout: the header, the arrangement timeline and the dock under it, the footer, and the dialogs and overlays that can open over any of them (search, report a problem, cut to length, the FMOD / Wwise package, Versions, the tour, the phone notice, project drops and shared links). |
| [`credits.ts`](../src/credits.ts) | Where every recorded instrument's samples come from, by the start of their address. The Credits in the guide are generated from this and the instrument list (`npm run guide-tables`), and a test fails if an instrument loads samples from a source that isn't listed here, or if the guide's tables are out of date. |
| [`main.tsx`](../src/main.tsx) | App entry point. Picks how the live audio context buffers (playbackMode.ts) before anything builds on it, then mounts the React app (the full studio, or Pocket, the phone version: see pocketMode.ts; each loads only its own interface) and starts the installed-app support (pwa.ts) and, in the phone app, its native pieces (nativeApp.ts, appLifecycle.ts). |
| [`version.ts`](../src/version.ts) | Which build of the app this is: its version (package.json, the top of CHANGELOG.md), the commit it was built from and when. Vite fills them in (vite.config.ts); outside a build (tests) they read "dev". |

## src/audio/

The sound engine. Everything that makes or measures sound: the master chain, the live graph, scheduling notes, audio clips and automation on the Transport, the offline export, the user's sound library, recording, metering, and the game, video and plugin exports. Files with no Web Audio in them (maths only) are unit-tested under Node.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`audioClipSchedule.ts`](../src/audio/audioClipSchedule.ts) | Audio clips (sound files on the timeline) on a Transport: each clip's sound plays from its offset with its gain, fades, crossfades, time-stretch and warp markers, into its track. Handles starts, seeks and loop passes into the middle of a clip. The same code serves live playback and every export render. |
| [`audioEdits.ts`](../src/audio/audioEdits.ts) | Edits of an audio clip that need its sound: reversing it, normalizing it and quantizing it. Each is one undo step. They work on the sound decoded at ANALYSIS_RATE. |
| [`auditionPart.ts`](../src/audio/auditionPart.ts) | Hearing a stretch of a sound straight away, outside the song (a chop in the Chop sample dialog, before it has a track): one buffer source through the master, gone when it ends. |
| [`automation.ts`](../src/audio/automation.ts) | Track automation maths, shared by the lane editor, the inspector and the audio scheduler (no audio here, so Node can unit-test it). |
| [`automationSchedule.ts`](../src/audio/automationSchedule.ts) | Automation lanes played as Web Audio parameter automation: each lane is written a short stretch ahead of the audio clock, so seeks, edits and loop wraps are heard almost at once without clicks. Live and in exports, one schedule per Transport. |
| [`beatPack.ts`](../src/audio/beatPack.ts) | The beat-store package producers sell a beat with, as pure pieces (no Web Audio, so Node tests them; BeatStoreDialog does the rendering): file names that carry the tempo and key, where a producer tag plays in the preview (at the start and/or every N seconds), and laying the tag over the beat with the beat dipped a little under it, so the tag is heard and the beat can't be used without it. |
| [`channelKit.ts`](../src/audio/channelKit.ts) | The channel kit: a song made into what a streamer, YouTuber or podcaster needs, in one .zip. - Intro and Outro, for the start and end of a video or a stream - three seamless loops for a stream's screens: Starting soon (the main part), Be right back (the same part without its lead, or without drums) and Ending (a calmer part) - three short alerts in the song's key and tempo (a follow, a subscribe, a big moment): the song's own stingers when it has some - a whoosh for a scene transition - a README saying what each file is for and how to use it in OBS and the like Which bars make each piece is planned in store/channelKit.ts. Everything is a WAV at 48 kHz (what streaming software and video runs at), 24-bit; the loops carry their loop points. The music is turned up or down to the loudness target by one gain for every piece (worked out on Starting soon), so a calmer piece stays calmer; no limiter, so the loops' seams stay seamless. |
| [`clipEnvelope.ts`](../src/audio/clipEnvelope.ts) | The loudness envelope of an audio clip: its gain and its fade in and fade out. Plain maths, so the player can pick the envelope up from any position (a seek into the middle of a clip) and Node can unit-test it. The player adds a short fade (DECLICK_SECONDS) wherever a clip is cut into its sound (a trimmed edge, a razor cut) and where playback starts or stops inside one, so cuts don't click; a clip that plays its sound from the very start, or to its end, is left as recorded, transients and all. |
| [`compressorLatency.ts`](../src/audio/compressorLatency.ts) | How long a browser compressor (DynamicsCompressorNode, which Tone.Compressor is) holds back the sound passing through it: its fixed look-ahead, about 6 ms, but it differs between browsers and sample rates, so it is measured rather than assumed. Once per sample rate, by sending a click through one in a tiny offline render and finding where it comes out; the answer is kept. |
| [`controlEvents.ts`](../src/audio/controlEvents.ts) | A plugin parameter's automation as timed events: the value a lane's writer holds, read on a fixed grid of the audio clock (every CONTROL_GRID samples, Fledge Synth's own control rate) and sent ahead as the plugin's timed parameter events, one where the value has moved. Live and in an export the same lane gives the same events (to within a grid step of where the song started on the clock), so a step lane's changes land on the sample, smoothed as its points say, whichever way it plays. Pure, so Node can test it (scripts/stepLanes.test.mjs). |
| [`delayCompensation.ts`](../src/audio/delayCompensation.ts) | Delay compensation: how much to hold back each track so every path through the mix reaches the master at the same moment. A compressor (the Compressor insert, the multiband one, the guitar amps' squeeze) looks ahead, so it holds back the sound passing through it by a few milliseconds; a compressed kick then landed a few ms after the uncompressed bass, which smeared them together. Pure (no Web Audio): the engine measures a compressor's delay and applies what this returns. |
| [`delayGlide.ts`](../src/audio/delayGlide.ts) | How a delay-compensation delay changes length while the music plays: it glides, slowly enough that the pitch bend can't be heard, rather than crossfading to the new length (see delayLink.ts, which plays it). Pure maths, so the tests can check the rate and that a new glide starts where the last one is. |
| [`driveCurves.ts`](../src/audio/driveCurves.ts) | Distortion curves for the heavy bass tools (the 808 designer and the Bass Drive insert): warm tube saturation, hard clipping, wave folding and bit crushing, each as a WaveShaper curve with the drive built in. Pure maths (no Web Audio), so Node tests check their shape and level. |
| [`dropLive.ts`](../src/audio/dropLive.ts) | The Drop pad, live: the Drop Pad instrument (its notes hold the master's effects, see effects/dropFx.ts) and the pads in Pocket tell the master's Drop worklet when each effect starts and stops, on the audio clock. The worklet is in the master chain only while the song has a Drop track (masterChain.ts); until it has loaded, nothing here sounds. |
| [`drumSynth.ts`](../src/audio/drumSynth.ts) | The Drum Designer's synth: renders a designed drum (src/store/drumDesign.ts) into samples, one hit at full velocity. Each layer is one voice: a kick's swept sine with a click, a snare's tone and wires, a clap's slaps and tail, a hat's six detuned square waves and noise, a rim, a tom, a shaker, a bell. Plain maths into a Float32Array, no Web Audio, so a hit renders the same in the app, in an export and in Node's tests; the noise comes from a seed (seededNoise.ts), so each hit's variation repeats exactly. |
| [`encoders.ts`](../src/audio/encoders.ts) | Audio file formats for exports. WAV is the exact one (and the only one with markers and loop points); MP3 and Ogg Vorbis are small, for sharing and for games (Godot and Unity both import Ogg Vorbis, and play it with a seamless loop). The encoders are the reference LAME and libvorbis compiled to WebAssembly (wasm-media-encoders), bundled into the app so they work offline. |
| [`endedDue.ts`](../src/audio/endedDue.ts) | Which sound sources' ended handlers an export runs at a suspend, and in what order (see endedOnTime.ts). Pure: no Web Audio. A source told to stop is due once the render has reached its stop time, whether or not the browser has reported its end yet (the report's moment varies from render to render; the stop time doesn't). One never told to stop is due once the browser has reported it. Due ones run in order of their stop times, then of when they were given a handler, so every render lets go of the same nodes in the same order. |
| [`endedOnTime.ts`](../src/audio/endedOnTime.ts) | "Ended" on time in an export: in an OfflineAudioContext marked with `endedOnTimeIn`, a sound source's ended handlers (onended and 'ended' listeners) run while the render is suspended, at the first suspend at or after the time the source was told to stop, not whenever the browser gets round to reporting it. The export calls `deliverEnded` at each of its suspends. |
| [`engine.ts`](../src/audio/engine.ts) | The master section and the live audio context. createMixChain builds the mix graph (master bus, compressor, the OTT and width inserts, the Level, the clipper, limiter and ceiling, plus the shared reverb and delay returns) in whatever context is current: once for live playback (liveMix) and again inside every export render. Also starting the audio, its running / suspended state, and the master volume. |
| [`enginePackage.ts`](../src/audio/enginePackage.ts) | The FMOD / Wwise package: the game kit's audio (every state as an exact loop and its stems, the stingers, the transition sounds) laid out for audio middleware, with - cues.json: the same description as the game kit's manifest, plus each state's place on one timeline (for FMOD's single-event layout); - fmod/Fledgetone_<song>.js: an FMOD Studio script (Scripts menu) that builds the event: a track per stem group, every state laid out with a loop region and a marker, the tempo, and an Intensity parameter driving each group's volume along its curve; - wwise/import_<song>.py: a Wwise Authoring API script that imports the states into a Music Switch Container (a playlist per state, a segment per loop, a track per stem), a State Group with a state per section, and an Intensity game parameter; - README.md: how to run them, and the steps each tool doesn't let a script do. The scripts try each step and say what worked, so a step a version of the tool doesn't support is reported rather than stopping the rest. |
| [`engineScripts.ts`](../src/audio/engineScripts.ts) | The FMOD and Wwise scripts and README for the engine package (see enginePackage.ts). No audio here, so Node can test them. |
| [`exactSums.ts`](../src/audio/exactSums.ts) | Exact sums in an export: every input (of a node or a parameter) of an OfflineAudioContext marked with `exactSumsIn` adds up its connections in an order that never changes, so the same song renders to the same samples every time (see sumChain.ts for why Chromium's own order varies, and how the links fix it). AudioNode's connect and disconnect are wrapped: in a marked context, the first connection into an input goes straight in as before, and each further one through a pass-through gain (see SumChain). Live playback and other contexts are untouched, as the order only changes the last bit of a sample. |
| [`exportLicence.ts`](../src/audio/exportLicence.ts) | The permission that travels with the files Fledgetone writes into exports (the game kit's players and example scenes, the FMOD and Wwise scripts, manifests): anyone may ship them inside any project, closed-source and paid games included, without opening their own code; but changes to these files themselves stay free (GPL), so nobody can take the tools and close them off (see TERMS.md, section 3). Each export that carries such files includes this text as LICENSE-exported-files.txt. |
| [`exportWav.ts`](../src/audio/exportWav.ts) | Offline rendering and WAV encoding. The arrangement (or its stems, an intro plus loop, loop takes, or one track for a freeze) is rendered faster than real time in an OfflineAudioContext, built from the same instrument, strip, schedule and master factories as live playback, so an export sounds like the app. Endings are ring-out, exact length or a seamless loop; WAVs are 16, 24 or 32-bit with markers as cue points and loop points. A mix is rendered in parts on several processor cores at once where that sounds exactly the same (see renderTracks and renderParts.ts). |
| [`gameKit.ts`](../src/audio/gameKit.ts) | The game kit: everything a game needs to play the song the way the Game preview does, in one .zip. Every state (section) as a seamless loop (and its stems), the stingers, the transitions, an audio_manifest.json describing them (tempo, bars, the transition rules, the intensity curves), and ready-made players for the web, Godot and Unity that read it and switch on the beat. |
| [`guitarStrum.ts`](../src/audio/guitarStrum.ts) | How a guitarist's hand plays a chord written as one block (all its notes at the same moment): the pick crosses the strings one after another, so the notes start a few milliseconds apart, low to high on a downstroke and high to low on an upstroke. A strum that follows another closely is the hand coming back up (strumming hands move down and up without stopping); one after a pause starts down again. A harder strum crosses the strings faster, a short chord is strummed quicker so it isn't smeared, and the strings the pick reaches last sound a little softer (an upstroke mostly catches the top strings, so its lowest are softer still). Every strum differs a little from the last (seeded from the chord and its time, so an export comes out the same every time). |
| [`hardTune.ts`](../src/audio/hardTune.ts) | Hard tune: the fast, robotic pitch correction of melodic rap and trap hooks, built on the vocal tuner (vocalTune.ts: YIN pitch, TD-PSOLA resynthesis). It adds what the robotic sound needs: - a Speed control from natural (0) to instant (100), mapped onto the tuner's glide time; - note holding (hysteresis) at fast speeds: a voice hovering half-way between two notes would otherwise flip between them every 10 ms, a warble rather than the clean step the effect is known for, so the note it's on is kept until the voice is clearly nearer another; - the scales such hooks are sung in (minor, harmonic minor, phrygian, minor pentatonic...). |
| [`hostedSets.ts`](../src/audio/hostedSets.ts) | The recordings hosted with the app, set by set (public/fledgetone-samples/<set>/): the MIDI notes each set has, how many loudness layers and takes every note has, the set's size in bytes and a fingerprint of its files. Generated by scripts/real-samples/convert.py; don't edit by hand. |
| [`human.ts`](../src/audio/human.ts) | The Human insert's maths: how far one note drifts from what's written, the way a player never hits the same note quite the same way twice. Nothing here is random at play time: each note's drift comes from a hash of its clip, its pitch and where it sits (noteSeed), so the song sounds the same on every play, in the WAV export and in a frozen track, yet no two notes are alike (a copied clip is a new clip, so it drifts differently from the one it was copied from). |
| [`index.ts`](../src/audio/index.ts) | The audio engine's entry point for the store (audioStore.ts: starting the audio, its state, the master volume), with the original synth instruments' factories and trigger helpers re-exported, and the chords, brass stabs and bass notes the retired sound deck's pads played. |
| [`instrumentCatalog.ts`](../src/audio/instrumentCatalog.ts) | Every instrument Fledgetone can play, in one place. The Add Track menu, the inspector, the piano roll's note range, the instrument menus and project validation all read this. |
| [`instrumentCatalogRetro.ts`](../src/audio/instrumentCatalogRetro.ts) | The retro instruments: the 1990s General MIDI soundfonts (FluidR3 and Musyng Kite, through midi-js-soundfonts) and the early tonejs-instruments recordings, all in one group. They're optional: every one is marked `retro`, and the instrument lists gather them under one Retro heading that stays hidden until "Show retro instruments" is on (see store/retroInstruments.ts), while songs that use them play them as they always did. Each keeps its group by sound (a pad is still a pad to the mixer and search); the ones a recording replaced outright are in the Retro group itself (see RECORDED in starters.ts for which). |
| [`instrumentPreview.ts`](../src/audio/instrumentPreview.ts) | Hear an instrument before choosing it: a short phrase on a dry copy of it (the same build and level a track gets, without any track's volume or effects), from the instrument menu's ▶ button. Pitched instruments play a rising arpeggio and a chord in the middle of their range; drum kits a short beat; sound effects a few of their sounds. |
| [`instruments.ts`](../src/audio/instruments.ts) | The TrackInstrument interface every instrument implements, and createInstrument, which builds any instrument in the catalog (synths, drum kits, recorded instruments, the Sampler, Slicer, Drum Rack, Multi Sampler, Synth Designer and plugins) in the current Tone context, with its level correction and high-note taper. Also the drum note map (DRUM_NOTES) and the expressive drum detune. |
| [`introSeam.ts`](../src/audio/introSeam.ts) | Where a game's intro runs into its loop (Intro + loop exports, renderIntroLoop in exportWav.ts): the intro's last few milliseconds crossfade into the loop's own last ones, so the intro's last sample leads into the loop's first exactly as the loop's last one does. |
| [`keptSounds.ts`](../src/audio/keptSounds.ts) | Sounds this browser keeps for itself, outside any project: the reference track, the producer tag. Each has a named slot holding a sound library id (the sound itself is in the library, in IndexedDB). They're never saved in a project or exported; freeing unused sounds leaves them be. |
| [`latency.ts`](../src/audio/latency.ts) | When the listener hears what the live context renders. The clock (currentTime) says what the graph is rendering now; the sound card plays that an output latency later. A note played in time with the music belongs where the music was heard, so live input and recording work in heard time (see heardTime). |
| [`legato.ts`](../src/audio/legato.ts) | Legato on the monophonic instruments: when a note joins the one before it (glides to it, or carries on without a new attack when it's the same pitch, a tie), and the order a legato plugin must hear the notes in. Pure logic, no Web Audio, so Node's tests cover it. |
| [`lineUp.ts`](../src/audio/lineUp.ts) | Lining up recording: the maths of measuring how late a microphone take arrives. A few soft clicks are played through the speaker and recorded with the microphone; where they turn up in the recording, against where they were played, is the round trip (the output's delay, the air, the input's delay) on this phone or computer. A take recorded later is moved back by that much (micRecorder.ts) instead of by the browser's own estimate, which is often off on phones. |
| [`lineUpRun.ts`](../src/audio/lineUpRun.ts) | Line up recording, once per setup (Pocket's vocal tool, the studio's recording settings): a few soft clicks are played through the speaker while the microphone records, and how late they arrive (lineUp.ts) is kept for this setup (micRecorder.ts). Takes recorded on it from then on are moved back by that measured delay instead of the browser's estimate. |
| [`liveContext.ts`](../src/audio/liveContext.ts) | The live audio context, its Transport and its output, shared by every module in place of Tone's global Tone.context / Tone.Transport / Tone.Destination. |
| [`liveInput.ts`](../src/audio/liveInput.ts) | Playing the timeline's instruments live: from a MIDI keyboard (Web MIDI) or the computer keyboard. Notes go to the armed track's instrument, or the selected track's when none is armed, through its channel strip, and are triggered straight on the audio clock (not through the Transport) so they sound at once. Whatever is played also goes to the take being recorded (recorder.ts), stamped with the audio time at which the listener heard it (latency.ts). |
| [`liveTracks.ts`](../src/audio/liveTracks.ts) | Live playback graph: one effects strip + one instrument per timeline track, kept in step with the store by syncLiveTracks(). The scheduler looks instruments up by track id at the moment a note plays, so swapping an instrument never needs a reschedule. |
| [`loudness.ts`](../src/audio/loudness.ts) | Loudness metering to ITU-R BS.1770-4 (what streaming services and broadcasters measure): momentary (400 ms), short-term (3 s) and integrated loudness in LUFS, K-weighted and gated, and the true peak in dBTP, found on a 4x oversampled signal so peaks between samples count. |
| [`loudnessMeter.ts`](../src/audio/loudnessMeter.ts) | The live loudness meter: an AudioWorklet (loudness.ts) listening to what the speakers get (after the master volume), posting ten readings a second. It exists only while something shows it (subscribeLoudness), so it costs nothing when hidden. The integrated loudness counts from the last Play (or Reset). |
| [`loudnessTarget.ts`](../src/audio/loudnessTarget.ts) | Loudness targets for exports: where the file is going (streaming, a club, a game, broadcast) sets how loud it should be. A file is turned up or down to its target; when getting there would push the peaks over the ceiling, the master limiter's kernel (effects/limiter.ts) holds them down instead, as a mastering engineer's limiter would, up to MAX_LIMITING_DB of gain reduction. |
| [`masterSpectrum.ts`](../src/audio/masterSpectrum.ts) | The master spectrum: an analyser listening to what the speakers get (after the master volume), for the spectrum readouts (spectrumSkins.ts). It's connected only while something shows it (watchMasterSpectrum), so it costs nothing when hidden. |
| [`metronome.ts`](../src/audio/metronome.ts) | The metronome: a click on every beat, accented on the first beat of a bar, straight to the live output (not through the master compressor and limiter, which it would otherwise pump). It lives on the live Transport only, so it can't reach a WAV export, which renders its own Transport in an OfflineAudioContext. Each click is a short oscillator made for that beat and gone after it, so a metronome that's off costs nothing, and one that's on costs a Transport event per beat. |
| [`micRecorder.ts`](../src/audio/micRecorder.ts) | Recording from a microphone (or any audio input) into the live context. The input is captured in blocks that carry their context time, so the first sample's place in the song is known exactly: the performer played along with music they heard an output latency after it was rendered, and their sound reached the graph an input latency after that, so both are taken off. Where recording has been lined up on this setup (lineUpRun.ts: clicks played and recorded), that measured round trip is taken off instead of the browser's estimate of the two. The input isn't sent to the speakers (no feedback through the mic). |
| [`microVariations.ts`](../src/audio/microVariations.ts) | Rendering micro-variations (the takes planned by src/store/microVariations.ts): each take played through the clip's track with its own pitch, brightness, note lengths and level, then trimmed and level-matched. |
| [`midi.ts`](../src/audio/midi.ts) | MIDI messages as the app understands them, and the computer keyboard's piano layout. Pure functions: the Web MIDI access and the live playing are in liveInput.ts. |
| [`mixAnalysis.ts`](../src/audio/mixAnalysis.ts) | Measuring a rendered mix (or a reference song, or one track's stem) for the Mix check and the reference A/B: its long-term average spectrum, middle and sides apart (where the low end sits in the stereo field), smoothed into fractional-octave bands, and short-term level envelopes of a frequency band (when the kick and the bass hit together). Plain maths on samples, no Web Audio, so Node can test it. |
| [`mixCheck.ts`](../src/audio/mixCheck.ts) | The Mix check: what a render of the song and of each track says about the mix, in plain words, with the track to look at where one is to blame. It looks for low end that isn't in the middle, kick and bass fighting, muddy low mids, harsh upper mids, a level that's wrong for where the song is going, a master section working too hard, and parts covering each other. |
| [`mixStudio.ts`](../src/audio/mixStudio.ts) | Rendering the song to study its mix: the Mix check (a render of the mix through the master section, and one of each track's stem, measured by mixAnalysis.ts and judged by mixCheck.ts), and the mix's loudness and spectrum that the reference track is matched and compared against (referenceTrack.ts). Kept in a small store of its own; nothing here is saved with the song. |
| [`nativeNodes.ts`](../src/audio/nativeNodes.ts) | Plain Web Audio nodes alongside Tone's. Tone's nodes are standardized-audio-context's wrappers around the browser's own; making nodes on the browser's context directly skips the wrapper's work (on every connect it walks the graph downstream, and some wrappers add nodes of their own), which matters for nodes made per note. These find the native context and nodes under Tone's, and keep a Tone node playing when only native nodes feed it. Used by plugins (wamHost.ts) and the recorded instruments (samplerManager.ts). |
| [`noteRepeat.ts`](../src/audio/noteRepeat.ts) | Note repeat, live: the pads held down with it on, each played again at the rate while it's held. A timer looks a little ahead and schedules each repeat on the audio clock: while the song plays, on the Transport's grid (the ticks a note drawn at that rate would have), so a repeat lands with the clips' notes and is recorded on its grid line; while it's stopped, every so many seconds at the song's tempo from the strike. Each repeat is recorded as a hit of its own (recorder.ts), its velocity the pad's pressure when the pad sends aftertouch (see repeatVelocity). |
| [`peq.ts`](../src/audio/peq.ts) | The parametric EQ's maths: each band is one Web Audio biquad, and this works out the same filter the browser runs (the Web Audio spec's formulas, from the Audio EQ Cookbook), so the curve drawn is the curve heard. No audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`perfMonitor.ts`](../src/audio/perfMonitor.ts) | Notices when playback can't keep up, and frees memory on request. |
| [`pitchShift.ts`](../src/audio/pitchShift.ts) | Re-pitching a recording without changing its length, for moving a sample into the song's key: time-stretch it (timeStretch.ts, same pitch) by the pitch ratio, then read the stretched copy back at that ratio, which puts the length back and moves the pitch. Plain arrays, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`playbackChoice.ts`](../src/audio/playbackChoice.ts) | The playback mode setting as it's stored in this browser (see playbackMode.ts): a mode the person picked, or Stable that the app switched to by itself after playback kept lagging (perfMonitor.ts). The app only ever switches by itself when nobody has picked a mode: a choice made on purpose, Responsive included, is kept. Pure, so Node can test it. |
| [`playbackMode.ts`](../src/audio/playbackMode.ts) | How the browser buffers live audio, chosen per browser (Inspector > Master > Playback) and applied when the app starts, before the mix is built (the browser fixes an audio context's buffer when it's created). Imported first by main.tsx. |
| [`producerTag.ts`](../src/audio/producerTag.ts) | The producer tag: a short sound (a voice saying the producer's name) laid over beat previews so they can't be used without paying. One slot, kept in this browser like the reference track (keptSounds.ts), never in a project. Everything that needs the tag asks here, so a fuller producer-tag feature can take over by changing only this file. |
| [`recorder.ts`](../src/audio/recorder.ts) | The take being recorded, if any: the live side of src/store/recording.ts. The store starts and ends takes with the Transport; the live input hands over what's played, with the audio time at which the listener heard it (see heardTime in latency.ts). Each note's song position is the live Transport's position at that time, so notes land where they were heard against the music, loop passes included. |
| [`recordingStore.ts`](../src/audio/recordingStore.ts) | The instruments' recordings, kept in this browser (IndexedDB) once downloaded, so each one is downloaded once ever: songs open at once on the next visit, and instruments already used work offline. IndexedDB rather than the Cache API because it also works when the app is opened from a file. A recording is stored under its address plus its set's fingerprint (`version`), so a re-made set is downloaded afresh rather than played from an old copy. |
| [`referenceTrack.ts`](../src/audio/referenceTrack.ts) | The reference track: a finished song loaded to compare the mix against. It's kept in this browser's sound library (keptSounds.ts), never in the project or an export. Its loudness is measured (loudness.ts) and it's played at the mix's loudness (the mix as last analysed, mixStudio.ts), so the comparison is about the sound, not the level; its spectrum is measured for the overlay. |
| [`renderBusy.ts`](../src/audio/renderBusy.ts) | How many offline renders (exports, stems, freezes) are running right now, so things that shouldn't interrupt one can wait for it: the update notice (pwa.ts) holds back until it's 0. |
| [`renderParts.ts`](../src/audio/renderParts.ts) | Splitting a mixdown into parts that render at the same time, each on its own processor core (see renderTracks in exportWav.ts): the tracks are split into parts whose sounds only meet at the master bus, each part's sound before the master section is rendered on its own, the parts are added up, and the master section runs once over the sum. No Web Audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`ringOutTail.ts`](../src/audio/ringOutTail.ts) | Where a ring-out export ends: once its tails have died away. The render runs long enough for the longest tail there can be (exportWav.ts: ringOutSeconds), then the file is cut where the mix last stood above RING_OUT_FLOOR_DB, plus the end fade. A fixed length cut drum and cymbal tails off at about -55 dB, while a short reverb left seconds of silence. Pure (samples in, a length out), so a render's file length is a function of its sound, and Node can test it. |
| [`runtimeKit.ts`](../src/audio/runtimeKit.ts) | The web runtime kit: for a web game where download size matters, the song as its project file (kilobytes) and bos-player.js, which synthesizes the music in the player's browser when the game loads (see src/runtime/player.ts), instead of megabytes of WAV files. With an example page and a README. |
| [`sampleAnalysis.ts`](../src/audio/sampleAnalysis.ts) | The tempo and key of a recording (a sample, a loop, an audio clip), heard from its sound, with how sure each guess is. Tempo: the onsets' spectral flux, autocorrelated, a comb over each candidate tempo's beat and bar, a gentle preference for the tempos beats are made at, then refined with the tempo finder (tempoFinder.ts) on the onsets and snapped to a whole number of bars when the sound is a loop. Key: a chroma profile (how strongly each of the 12 pitch classes sounds, from the spectrum's peaks, after measuring how far the recording sits from A440) matched against the major and minor key templates (songKey.ts). Plain arrays, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`sampleAnalysisStore.ts`](../src/audio/sampleAnalysisStore.ts) | The tempo and key of the sounds in the library (sampleAnalysis.ts), worked out once per sound when something on screen asks, in idle time, and remembered in this browser by the sound's id (a hash of its bytes, so the same file always has the same answer). |
| [`sampleTuning.ts`](../src/audio/sampleTuning.ts) | Tuning corrections for the recorded instruments, measured. Each recording's pitch was read two ways (by its period, YIN, and from its harmonics; voices by their period only) over the loud part of the note, then refined from chromatic scales rendered through the app: the keys that play from one recording give its remaining error, and their median sets its correction. - `cents`: how far to re-pitch a recording when it loads (positive raises it). - `notes`: for soundfont instruments, which recordings to use (the soundfonts have every semitone; a steadier one a semitone away replaces a wobbly or badly tuned one). Bells, drums and the piano (whose stretched tuning is deliberate) aren't corrected. |
| [`scheduler.ts`](../src/audio/scheduler.ts) | Note clips to Transport events. createClipSchedule plays every note clip on a Transport (one event per tick that has notes, shared by all clips and tracks, updated incrementally as clips change), live and in exports; each note group goes to its track's instrument, looked up when it plays. Also applies the loop region, tempo and swing to the live Transport (syncTransport). |
| [`seededNoise.ts`](../src/audio/seededNoise.ts) | Repeatable noise for the instruments, so a song renders the same sample for sample every time. The noise buffers are filled from a fixed seed, and each noise burst starts at a point of its looped buffer picked by a hash of its key (its track, what plays it: a drum row, a note, which layer) and its time. Every burst still differs from the next, as a drum never sounds quite the same twice; it just differs the same way on every play and in every export. (Before, the buffers and starting points came from Math.random: two exports of a song with a riser or a clap in it nulled to only about -17 dB.) |
| [`showcaseDraw.ts`](../src/audio/showcaseDraw.ts) | The Showcase picture for the MP4 export: the song's notes on a piano roll that scrolls past a red playhead, as on fledgetone.com's home page. A note lights up as the playhead reaches it (with sparkles, rings or just its glow), glows while it's held and dims once it's played. |
| [`slicerTools.ts`](../src/audio/slicerTools.ts) | Slicing a sound the browser has decoded: the Slicer's Auto mode and "Chop to Slicer" need the sound's energy envelope, worked out once per decoded buffer and kept with it. |
| [`slicing.ts`](../src/audio/slicing.ts) | Cutting a sound into slices for the Slicer: equal parts, or at the transients found in its energy envelope. Plain maths on arrays, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`soundLibrary.ts`](../src/audio/soundLibrary.ts) | The user's own sound files (audio clips, the Sampler, the Slicer, the Drum Rack and the Multi Sampler). They're kept in this browser's IndexedDB under a hash of their bytes, decoded once per sample rate, measured for waveform peaks in idle time, cached as time-stretched or warped copies, and embedded into saved project files. |
| [`soundfontSets.ts`](../src/audio/soundfontSets.ts) | The note-name and sample-map helpers for the older sample sets: the General MIDI soundfonts rendered by midi-js-soundfonts (FluidR3_GM, MusyngKite), whose instruments are in instrumentCatalogRetro.ts, and the tonejs-instruments recordings. Kept apart from instrumentCatalog.ts so the retro catalog can use them without the two importing each other. |
| [`spectrumSkins.ts`](../src/audio/spectrumSkins.ts) | Spectrum readouts: the sound's frequency bands (0 to 1 each, lows first) drawn as LED bars or as a cyberpunk scene that moves with the music. The same drawings are used live (the visualizer in the Mixer tab) and in the MP4 video export, so a video looks like the app. |
| [`stingerPlayer.ts`](../src/audio/stingerPlayer.ts) | Stingers out loud: fired over the music in the Game preview, on the next beat or bar the way a game would, and rendered to WAV files for the export. |
| [`subLayer.ts`](../src/audio/subLayer.ts) | The Sub enhancer (Track.subLayer): a clean sine played under a track's own notes, an octave down or on the note itself, so a thin bass gets a solid, mono floor. It follows the notes rather than the sound (there's no reliable way to find an octave below a sound without an audio worklet, which would slow every export), so it's exact: in tune, in time, the same live and exported. One sine at a time (the lowest note of a chord), sliding between overlapping notes. |
| [`sumChain.ts`](../src/audio/sumChain.ts) | The wiring of an exact sum: how three or more connections into one input (of a node or a parameter) are added up in an order that never changes, so a song renders the same sample for sample every time. Pure bookkeeping on handles, no Web Audio: exactSums.ts carries out the connects and disconnects it returns. |
| [`tempoMap.ts`](../src/audio/tempoMap.ts) | The song's tempo map and meter map: tempo changes (a jump, or a glide from the tempo before) and time-signature changes along the timeline. |
| [`timeStretch.ts`](../src/audio/timeStretch.ts) | Time-stretching: play a recording faster or slower without changing its pitch, so an audio clip can follow the song's tempo. WSOLA (waveform-similarity overlap-add): the output is built from short overlapping windows of the input, each taken from about where it should be, nudged to where its waveform best continues the window before, so the joins don't beat or click. Good on drums, loops and voices at the small changes tempo edits make (it smears sharp hits a little beyond about ±30%). Plain arrays, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`timecode.ts`](../src/audio/timecode.ts) | Timecode arithmetic on whole frames, independent of tempo and Tone.js (so Node can unit-test it). |
| [`toneFixes.ts`](../src/audio/toneFixes.ts) | Fixes for Tone.js behaviour that breaks this app, applied when the module is imported (engine.ts imports it before any oscillator exists). See each fix's comment below. |
| [`transport.ts`](../src/audio/transport.ts) | Positions and time on a Transport: 1-based bars to Tone ticks and back, the song's meter and the live tempo map, swing, and where playback is (what's been scheduled versus what the listener hears now). |
| [`videoExport.ts`](../src/audio/videoExport.ts) | A song as an MP4 video, for YouTube, socials or a game's trailer: the rendered mix as its sound, and a visualizer as its picture (the project's name, a spectrum that moves with the music, the whole song's waveform with a playhead, the section it's in, the time). Encoded faster than real time with the browser's own encoders (WebCodecs) and put into an MP4 by Mediabunny. |
| [`vocalDouble.ts`](../src/audio/vocalDouble.ts) | Double a vocal take: two new performances of it, one for the left and one for the right, each a little early or late and a few cents sharp or flat, as a rapper's doubles are when they're sung again rather than copied (an exact copy only makes the take louder). Played under the lead, lower, they thicken and widen it. |
| [`vocalTune.ts`](../src/audio/vocalTune.ts) | Vocal tuning: find the pitch a voice (or any one-note-at-a-time instrument) is singing, pull it towards the nearest note of the song's key, and sing it again at the corrected pitch with its timing, length and character unchanged. |
| [`waitFor.ts`](../src/audio/waitFor.ts) | Waiting with a limit: a promise that gives up after a while, and a download that gives up when no bytes have come for a while (a stuck connection, which the browser itself can wait on for minutes). Either way the timer and the listeners are let go, so nothing is left behind. Also a download's address with its set's fingerprint (versionedUrl). No audio engine here, so Node can test it; recordingStore.ts and exportWav.ts use it. |
| [`wamHost.ts`](../src/audio/wamHost.ts) | Hosting Web Audio Modules (WAM 2.0): third-party instruments and effects, each an ES module at a URL whose default export is a WebAudioModule. A plugin runs in the native audio context (the live one, or an export's offline one) and is wired into Tone's graph through the native nodes Tone's wrappers keep. Plugins are code from elsewhere, so one named by an opened project only loads once the person has allowed its URL (adding a plugin yourself allows it). The app's own built-in plugins (`builtin:` addresses) are made by plugins/builtinHost.ts instead. |
| [`wavCues.ts`](../src/audio/wavCues.ts) | Markers in an exported WAV, as cue points: a `cue ` chunk with each one's sample position and a `LIST`/`adtl` chunk of `labl` names, the standard RIFF way to mark a WAV, which DAWs, audio editors and game audio tools read as markers. No audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`wavFile.ts`](../src/audio/wavFile.ts) | A WAV file from rendered channels: 16- or 24-bit PCM (16-bit with a quiet TPDF dither), or 32-bit float, with cue points and loop points after the audio. No audio engine here, so Node can unit-test it; exportWav.ts and the game kit write their files with it. |
| [`waveform.ts`](../src/audio/waveform.ts) | Waveform overviews: a sound's peaks, worked out once and kept, and the SVG path that draws any stretch of them at any width. No audio nodes here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`worklets.ts`](../src/audio/worklets.ts) | AudioWorklet modules by context. The processors' code lives in strings (ott.ts, loudness.ts), loaded through a Blob URL so the one-file build needs no extra file. Each module is added once per audio context (the live one, and each WAV export's offline one); Tone's own addAudioWorkletModule remembers only one module per context, so this keeps its own list. |
| [`zip.ts`](../src/audio/zip.ts) | A minimal .zip writer for bundling exported stems into one download. Files are STOREd (not compressed): WAV audio barely compresses, and storing keeps this small and fast. The file data stays in its Blobs; only the headers are built here. |

## src/audio/effects/

Effects: the per-track channel strip and its inserts, the shared reverb and delay, the master inserts, and the parameter writer that keeps automation and controls from fighting.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`bassDrive.ts`](../src/audio/effects/bassDrive.ts) | The Bass Drive insert: the standard heavy-bass trick of distorting a bass's mids and highs while its sub stays clean. The sound is split at the crossover by a Linkwitz-Riley pair (two Butterworth low-passes against two high-passes: put back together they sum flat). Below it: folded to mono and passed through untouched. Above it: distorted (4x oversampled, so the harmonics the clipping makes above hearing don't fold back down as fizz), darkened by a tone low-pass, cut below the crossover again (distortion's difference tones would land in the sub), and mixed with the clean highs. |
| [`busEffects.ts`](../src/audio/effects/busEffects.ts) | Shared return effects fed by every track's post-fader sends: one reverb and one ping-pong delay. One instance of each keeps CPU low however many tracks there are. Built per context (live, and again inside the offline export render). |
| [`busInserts.ts`](../src/audio/effects/busInserts.ts) | Two lean inserts for group buses (and any track): Saturation, a warm full-range soft clip that thickens and glues (unlike the Distortion, it keeps the lows: a kick or 808 keeps its weight), and Mono bass, which puts everything under a crossover in the middle, as an 808 or bass bus wants. Each is a handful of native nodes, built only while switched on (see trackStrip.ts), so live and export run the same nodes. |
| [`clipper.ts`](../src/audio/effects/clipper.ts) | The master clipper: the mix driven into a soft or hard clipper just before the limiter, the way loud rap and electronic masters shave their tallest drum peaks off so the limiter has less to do (it squashes the whole mix where a clipper only touches the peaks). It is oversampled four times, so the corners clipping puts on a wave don't fold back down as harsh, out-of-tune aliasing. |
| [`delayLink.ts`](../src/audio/effects/delayLink.ts) | A connection that can hold the sound back by a few milliseconds and change how much while it plays, without a click: the track strip's paths after its sends are taken (delay compensation, see delayCompensation.ts). |
| [`distance.ts`](../src/audio/effects/distance.ts) | Distance (Track.distance): how a part set back on the stage reaches the hall. Its reverb send gets a little more on top of what the track sends, whether the send is the track's own setting or an automation lane's value at the moment (the lane writes the send, so the extra is added to each value it writes). Pure numbers, so Node can test it; trackStrip.ts applies them. |
| [`dropFx.ts`](../src/audio/effects/dropFx.ts) | The Drop pad's effects: what a DJ does to the whole mix with a finger, held for as long as the pad is held and in time with the song. Stutter repeats the 16th that was playing; Filter sweeps the mix down to a muffle over a bar; Tape stop slows it to a halt over a beat; Crush makes it gritty and lo-fi; Gate chops it into 16ths; Echo throws what's playing into a dotted-8th echo that rings on after letting go. Several can be held at once. |
| [`lightFx.ts`](../src/audio/effects/lightFx.ts) | Lean stand-ins for Tone.EQ3, Tone.Distortion and Tone.Chorus that sound the same but cost far less CPU, and the track Filter and Pump built the same way. |
| [`limiter.ts`](../src/audio/effects/limiter.ts) | The master limiter: a look-ahead, true-peak brickwall. The sound is delayed a little (its `latency`, about 5 ms); meanwhile each incoming sample's peak, including the peaks between samples that a DAC or an MP3 encoder will reconstruct, sets the gain it needs to stay under the ceiling. The peaks between samples are found with the same 4x interpolation filter a true-peak meter uses (ITU-R BS.1770, as loudness.ts measures exports): a simpler estimate (cubic interpolation) missed up to half a dB on bright, dense mixes, so they passed the ceiling. The gain is the lowest needed over the look-ahead window, eased back up afterwards (the release) and smoothed with a moving average as long as the window, so it has always come down by the time the peak plays, without a click. Both channels share one gain, so the stereo image doesn't shift. |
| [`lushAfter.ts`](../src/audio/effects/lushAfter.ts) | The lush reverb run in plain JavaScript over an export's reverb sends, after the render: the shared reverb's input filters (the low cut and the damping that busEffects.ts puts before every room) and the lush kernel (lushReverb.ts), as the live graph runs them. |
| [`lushReverb.ts`](../src/audio/effects/lushReverb.ts) | The "Lush" master reverb: an algorithmic room (a feedback delay network) run as an AudioWorklet, in place of the convolver. A long convolution costs the computer more the longer its tail, and runs even in silence; this costs the same at any decay, a fraction of it, and rests when nothing is playing. Its tail is smooth, dense and gently moving. |
| [`masterAfter.ts`](../src/audio/effects/masterAfter.ts) | The master section after the master compressor, run in plain JavaScript over an export's finished render: the OTT, the stereo width, the Drop pad's effects, the Level, the clipper, then the look-ahead limiter, in the order the live graph has them (engine.ts, masterChain.ts). The master compressor (the glue, a native DynamicsCompressorNode) stays in the render; the render stops after it. |
| [`masterChain.ts`](../src/audio/effects/masterChain.ts) | The master section's inserts, between the master compressor and the Level and limiter (see engine.ts): compressor -> [OTT] -> [Stereo width] -> [Drop] -> Level -> [Clipper] -> limiter The Drop pad's effects (dropFx.ts) are there only while the song has a Drop track (setDrop). Each insert exists only while it's switched on, like a track's inserts: off, it is taken out of the chain and disposed, so it costs nothing. The OTT is an AudioWorklet (ott.ts); the width is a handful of plain nodes doing mid/side; the Level is one gain, always there. A switch crossfades between the old and the new chain on the audio clock the way a track strip does (trackStrip.ts, rewire), so switching while the song plays opens no gap. |
| [`ott.ts`](../src/audio/effects/ott.ts) | OTT: the "over the top" multiband compressor of modern bass music. The sound is split into three bands (below 120 Hz, 120 Hz to 2.5 kHz, above), and each band is compressed both ways: loud parts are turned down (downward compression) and quiet parts turned up (upward compression), so every band sits at a steady level however the mix moves. That flattens a mix, brings up reverb tails and detail, and makes basses and supersaws dense and bright. |
| [`paramWriter.ts`](../src/audio/effects/paramWriter.ts) | Every change to one native AudioParam, written so that no change ever cuts another off midway. |
| [`roomIR.ts`](../src/audio/effects/roomIR.ts) | Designed reverb impulse responses for the shared reverb, one per room style. Tone.Reverb's own is white noise fading at one rate, which sounds like a hiss in a tunnel; a real room is different at every frequency (the air and the walls soak up the highs, so they die first, and big rooms keep their lows longest), answers first with a few distinct early reflections off the nearest walls, and reaches each ear differently. Each style sets those: how long before the first reflection, the reflections' pattern, how quickly the tail builds up, and how much longer or shorter its lows and highs ring than its middle. The `decay` (seconds) is the middle's. |
| [`smoothParam.ts`](../src/audio/effects/smoothParam.ts) | Moving a parameter that is sounding without a click: every control the user turns while the music plays (a mix, a drive, a band of the EQ, a mute, a solo) goes to its new value through smoothSet, a short glide that starts from wherever the param is at that moment. |
| [`spaceFx.ts`](../src/audio/effects/spaceFx.ts) | The Delay and Reverb inserts: a track's own echoes and room, as against the shared master reverb and delay its sends feed. On a return track at full mix they are a return's effect, fed by any track's send. Both are built from plain Web Audio nodes, like lightFx.ts. |
| [`trackStrip.ts`](../src/audio/effects/trackStrip.ts) | The mixer channel each track plays through: its inserts (in the order listed on TrackStrip), a stereo balance pan, solo and mute, the fader, and post-fader sends to the shared reverb and delay and to return tracks. An insert exists only while it's switched on, so idle effects cost nothing. Also the Pump's beat clock (createPumpClock). |

## src/audio/plugins/

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`builtinHost.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/builtinHost.ts) | Built-in plugins: open-source effects and instruments compiled to WebAssembly (see scripts/plugins/), hosted next to the page in fledgetone-plugins/ and downloaded the first time one of their family is used (then kept in this browser, like the instruments' recordings). |
| [`fledgeLayout.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/fledgeLayout.ts) | Fledge Synth's settings as its editor (FledgeSynthPanel.tsx) lays them out: each control names the engine's parameter (engine/fledge-synth/src/params.rs), and the panel finds its index from the names the plugin reports. Choices carry their list and its room to grow (`cap`: the stored 0..1 is the option's place out of cap). scripts/plugins.test.mjs checks all of this against the engine itself, so the two can't drift apart. |
| [`fledgeMacros.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/fledgeMacros.ts) | Fledge Synth's macros and wobble in plain words: the presets in the engine's order, a short name for what each preset's macros move ("Speed up", "Growl", "Grit"), what a macro moves read from the matrix (slots 5 to 8 in the presets), and which LFO is the wobble (the first one in time with the song that moves something), with the tempo divisions offered for it. The studio panel (FledgeSynthPanel.tsx) and Pocket's Sound tool (PocketSynth.tsx) both use these; scripts/fledgeMacros.test.mjs checks them against the engine. |
| [`fledgeWave.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/fledgeWave.ts) | Fledge Synth's oscillator pictures, drawn by the synth's own code: a copy of its WebAssembly on the main thread (the playing one is on the audio thread) answers fledge_wave, one cycle of a table at a position under a warp. |
| [`paramNames.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/paramNames.ts) | The parameter names of each built-in plugin (by its address), as its instances report them when they start, live or in an export. Step lanes (store/stepLanes.ts) name a plugin's parameter ("Macro 1") rather than its number, which can change between versions of a plugin; this is how the store finds the number for the track's own setting of it. No audio here, so Node can test what uses it. |
| [`pluginCatalog.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/pluginCatalog.ts) | The built-in plugins, by family (generated by scripts/plugins/catalog.mjs from the compiled families: don't edit). |
| [`pluginCatalogGpl.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/pluginCatalogGpl.ts) | The built-in plugins, by family (generated by scripts/plugins/catalog.mjs from the compiled families: don't edit). |
| [`pluginSources.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/pluginSources.ts) | Builds that include the GPL-licensed plugins (see builtinHost.ts): VITE_GPL_PLUGINS=1. |
| [`pluginTypes.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/pluginTypes.ts) | A built-in plugin family: one WebAssembly module holding many plugins (see scripts/plugins/). |
| [`processor.ts`](../src/audio/plugins/processor.ts) | The AudioWorklet processor that runs built-in plugins (see builtinHost.ts). Each plugin family is one WebAssembly module (scripts/plugins/bbplug.h is its interface); the first plugin of a family in a context instantiates it, and every plugin of that family in the context then lives in that one instance's memory. |

## src/audio/presets/

The instruments' sound design: one factory per instrument (or family), each building its nodes in whatever audio context is current, so the export can rebuild the same sound offline.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`bass.ts`](../src/audio/presets/bass.ts) | Funk Slap Bass (Monophonic) Tight slap/squelch bass with fast transient attack and resonant filter sweep. Built by a factory so offline (WAV export) rendering can recreate it in its own context. |
| [`bass808Designer.ts`](../src/audio/presets/bass808Designer.ts) | The designed 808 (an 808 Bass track with Track.bass808 set; see bass808.ts): a sine with a pitch-drop punch, a decay, slides between overlapping notes, distortion with a tone control after it, and a top layer of harmonics for small speakers. Plain Web Audio nodes per note (see native.ts), so nothing runs between notes. A new setting plays from the next note. |
| [`brass.ts`](../src/audio/presets/brass.ts) | Funk Brass Stabs (Polyphonic) Punchy 70s/80s horn section stabs with filter swell. Built by a factory so offline (WAV export) rendering can recreate it in its own context. |
| [`chiptune.ts`](../src/audio/presets/chiptune.ts) | Chiptune: the sound chips of 8-bit consoles, as plain Web Audio nodes (see native.ts). - Chip Lead: a 25% pulse wave (the classic 8-bit console lead), a hard gate, and a vibrato that comes in after the note has sounded a moment. - Chip Bass: the 4-bit stepped triangle those chips played bass lines on: no volume envelope (the real one had none), so it's gated on and off. - Chip Drums: a pitch-swept kick, noise snare and hats, and a "metallic" periodic noise for the open hat and the cowbell, the way the chips' noise channel sounded in its short mode. |
| [`designedKit.ts`](../src/audio/presets/designedKit.ts) | The Designed Kit: every drum row plays the sound designed for it in the Drum Designer (Track.drumDesign, or the row's default preset). Each row's sound is rendered once, in plain maths (drumSynth.ts), at the rate of the context it plays in, and kept; a hit is one buffer source and one gain, so a dense hat roll costs next to nothing, and the same buffer plays live and in an export, so the two sound exactly alike. Changing a sound renders that row again at its next hit (the others are kept). |
| [`designer.ts`](../src/audio/presets/designer.ts) | Harmonics (amplitude by number, from 1) of the table waves (see OscWave). |
| [`drums.ts`](../src/audio/presets/drums.ts) | Groove Drum Kit (Synthesized Analog Drums) 1. Kick: Punchy 909-style sub-transient membrane 2. Snare / Clap: Layered white noise with 800Hz highpass filter + 200Hz pitched snap 3. Hi-Hat: Metallic FM percussion with closed (0.05s) and open (0.28s) decay 4. Funk Cowbell: High-pitched punchy square wave at 800Hz |
| [`edmBass.ts`](../src/audio/presets/edmBass.ts) | The EDM basses: Wobble, Growl and Reese. Monophonic, built from plain Web Audio nodes per note (see native.ts), with a short glide when a note starts before the previous one has ended. |
| [`edmSynths.ts`](../src/audio/presets/edmSynths.ts) | The EDM poly synths: Supersaw and Pluck. Every note is its own handful of plain Web Audio nodes (see native.ts), so there's no voice limit to drop notes at and nothing runs between notes. |
| [`fx.ts`](../src/audio/presets/fx.ts) | The FX instrument: one transition effect per row (FX_ROWS). Risers, sweeps, the reverse crash, the sub drop and the downlifter stretch to the length of the note (draw a 4-bar note for a 4-bar riser); Impact is a one-shot whatever its length. Each hit is plain Web Audio nodes built for that note (see native.ts), its sweeps scheduled with it. |
| [`keys.ts`](../src/audio/presets/keys.ts) | Space Clav / Electric Keys (Polyphonic) Lush vintage FM keys / funk clavinet with stereo chorus and silky room reverb. Built by a factory so offline (WAV export) rendering can recreate it in its own context. `ready` resolves once the reverb impulse response has been generated. |
| [`kitExtras.ts`](../src/audio/presets/kitExtras.ts) | The drum rows past the original five (clap, three toms, crash, ride), synthesized from plain Web Audio nodes so every kit has them: the synthesized kits use all of them, the recorded kits the ones their library has no recording of. |
| [`monotonic.ts`](../src/audio/presets/monotonic.ts) | Monophonic Tone synths throw if triggered twice at the same instant ("Start time must be strictly greater than previous start time"), which happens when overlapping clips land hits on one tick. Each voice gets one of these to nudge a repeat hit 1 ms later instead of crashing the scheduler callback. |
| [`native.ts`](../src/audio/presets/native.ts) | Building blocks for instruments made of plain Web Audio nodes, created for each note and let go when it ends (the EDM synths and the FX instrument). Nothing of theirs runs between notes. Tone's envelopes, LFOs and filters are the opposite: their ConstantSourceNodes (and, for Tone.Filter, per-sample filter coefficients) keep the audio thread busy whether anything plays or not. Envelopes and sweeps are parameter automation scheduled with the note, so they are sample-accurate live and in the WAV export alike. |
| [`poly.ts`](../src/audio/presets/poly.ts) | A polyphonic synth made from a pool of monophonic Tone voices (createVoicePool), used instead of Tone.PolySynth: voices are added as needed instead of notes being dropped, and silent ones are freed. |
| [`sampleKits.ts`](../src/audio/presets/sampleKits.ts) | The Drum Rack and the Multi Sampler: the user's own sounds played from buffers, each hit or note a buffer source and a gain made when it starts and let go when it ends (nothing runs between them). Live and in the WAV export alike; `ready` waits for every sound to be decoded. |
| [`sampledKit.ts`](../src/audio/presets/sampledKit.ts) | A recorded drum kit: the recordings of each drum row (see the catalog's `samples`, keyed by the rows' note names), played as they are, never pitched. A kit recorded at several loudnesses and takes ("<note>\|<layer>\|<take>", see SampleSource.layers) plays the recording for each hit's velocity, its takes in turn, as a drummer never hits the same way twice. Rows the kit has no recording of are left to the synthesized extras (kitExtras.ts). |
| [`slicer.ts`](../src/audio/presets/slicer.ts) | The Slicer instrument (vocal chops): a sound cut into slices, one per key from C3 up, each note playing its slice from a buffer with a short fade at either end. |
| [`synths.ts`](../src/audio/presets/synths.ts) | The Tone.js synth instruments: the Wavetable pad, Sub-Bass, the 808 (with slides between overlapping notes, and the modern two-layer version for expressive tracks), the Analog Lead and the Drum Machine kit. |
| [`wamPlugin.ts`](../src/audio/presets/wamPlugin.ts) | Web Audio Module plugins in the mix: a Plugin track's instrument (createPluginInstrument) and the plugin effects on a track (createPluginChain). Loading, permission and the plugin's own window are in wamHost.ts and PluginDialogs.tsx. |
| [`widen.ts`](../src/audio/presets/widen.ts) | A gentle stereo widener for the instruments that would otherwise play in mono (the pads and leads): a copy of the sound a few milliseconds late, its lows cut, is added to the left and taken from the right. Each side then rings at slightly different frequencies, which the ear hears as width, while left plus right is exactly the sound as it was, so nothing is lost or hollowed out when the song is played in mono (a phone speaker, a club's mono sub). Plain Web Audio nodes with fixed settings: they cost next to nothing while the instrument is quiet. |

## src/audio/samplers/

Recorded instruments: downloading, decoding and playing multi-sampled recordings, with tone shaping, guitar amps and expressive playing.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`layerBlend.ts`](../src/audio/samplers/layerBlend.ts) | How a recorded instrument blends two of a note's loudnesses (near a loudness boundary, or under the mod wheel): the softer recording's and the louder one's levels across the blend. Pure, so Node can test it; samplerManager.ts uses it. |
| [`noteStealing.ts`](../src/audio/samplers/noteStealing.ts) | Which note to let go when an instrument has too many sounding: the one quietest now, not the oldest. A long-held chord under fast runs used to lose its oldest notes first, often the ones still ringing loudest, while the last run's notes, already faded to a whisper, played on. |
| [`recordingMaths.ts`](../src/audio/samplers/recordingMaths.ts) | Maths on a recording's samples as it loads, to keep it small in memory without changing how it sounds: where its silent tail can be cut, whether its two channels are one sound twice (a mono recording saved as stereo, as many soundfont files are), and a coarse outline of its level over time (for choosing which note to let go when too many sound: see noteStealing.ts). Also lengthening a recording that stops dead, and the stretch of it that loops for a note held longer, and taking out the DC some recordings carry. |
| [`samplerManager.ts`](../src/audio/samplers/samplerManager.ts) | Sampled instruments. Each instrument's recordings are downloaded and decoded once, then shared by every sampler that plays it: each track's own sampler, the instrument menus' preview sampler, and the offline export (AudioBuffers aren't tied to a context). |
| [`songSamples.ts`](../src/audio/samplers/songSamples.ts) | Which of a recorded instrument's recordings a song needs first: for each note it plays, the recording nearest that pitch (the one the sampler would pick) at every loudness its velocity can reach, every take of those, the next recording on the other side within stretching distance, and the release sounds nearest it. The instrument loads these first and plays as soon as they're in; the rest follow in the background (see samplerManager.ts). |

## src/audio/sfx/

The sound effects maker's synth (plain maths, no Web Audio).

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`sfxModern.ts`](../src/audio/sfx/sfxModern.ts) | The modern sound effects engine's parts (sfxSynth.ts uses them for a sound with `modern` on; a classic sound renders as it always has): - band-limited square and saw (PolyBLEP), so high notes don't fold back into gritty tones; - material bodies: a struck object simulated by its resonances (modes), each a decaying two-pole resonator, with the mode ratios, levels and ring times of wood, metal, glass, stone, plastic or a stretched skin, so a hit sounds like the thing that was hit; - recordings: public-domain foley (footsteps, cloth, water, debris...) played as a layer, from a registry the app fills when they've loaded (sfxRecordings.ts), so this file stays pure; - a stereo space: early reflections, then a stereo reverb (Freeverb, the right channel's delays a little longer), and a ping-pong echo. Plain arrays in and out, so Node can test it. |
| [`sfxRecordingSets.ts`](../src/audio/sfx/sfxRecordingSets.ts) | The recordings the sound effects maker layers under its modern sounds (public/fledgetone-sfx/ <group>/<take>.mp3), group by group: its label, how many takes, each take's length (seconds), whether it's a loop, its size and a fingerprint of its files. Public-domain (CC0) foley; who made it: public/fledgetone-sfx/README.txt. Generated by scripts/sfx-recordings/build.py; don't edit by hand. |
| [`sfxRecordings.ts`](../src/audio/sfx/sfxRecordings.ts) | Loads the recordings modern sounds layer (sfxRecordingSets.ts; public/fledgetone-sfx/) when a sound needs them, and hands them to the synth (sfxModern.setSfxRecordings). A sound renders without a recording that hasn't loaded yet (that layer is silent), so whatever renders a sound for keeps (an export, the game kit, the maker's preview) awaits ensureSfxRecordings first. Every take of a group loads at once, since each variation of a sound picks a different one. |
| [`sfxSynth.ts`](../src/audio/sfx/sfxSynth.ts) | The sound effects maker's synth: game sounds from a few layers of simple sources (waves, noise, FM, bells, crackle), each with its own pitch movement, filter and envelope, then drive, echo and reverb over the whole. About sixty kinds of sound (retro, UI, combat, movement, rewards, magic and sci-fi, jingles, ambience loops) each have a recipe that rolls new settings from a seed, so the same seed always gives the same sound. A set (a game's UI sounds, say) shares a style seed, so its sounds belong together. Sounds are levelled to a loudness for their kind, trimmed and faded; loops render seamless. Rendering is plain maths into a Float32Array, with no Web Audio, so Node can unit-test it and the files are the same everywhere. |

## src/components/

The React UI outside the timeline: the header, the instrument menu, popovers, and shared controls.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`Header.tsx`](../src/components/Header.tsx) | The header bar: the menu bar, the project bar (name, Save, Export, Share), tempo, Fit to time and swing, the intensity slider, master volume, the loudness and performance badges, and the Search, Learn, Guide and Start Audio buttons. Also the ? shortcut that opens the guide. |
| [`InstrumentMenu.tsx`](../src/components/InstrumentMenu.tsx) | Choosing an instrument by typing: a search field over the instrument list. With nothing typed the list is grouped as in the catalog; typing narrows it to the best matches first (by name, then by style or mood words like "8-bit", "angelic" or "orchestral", then by description). Up and Down move through it, Enter picks. The retro instruments (1990s soundfonts) are left out unless shown (a switch at the bottom), except the one a track already plays. Starred instruments are listed first under Favourites, and where a list can take them, the sounds you've saved (mySounds.ts) above those, under My sounds. |
| [`LoudnessBadge.tsx`](../src/components/LoudnessBadge.tsx) | The loudness readout in the header: short-term LUFS while audio runs, red once the true peak passes -1 dBTP. |
| [`MobileNotice.tsx`](../src/components/MobileNotice.tsx) | The notice on phones that the studio is made for a computer, with the way to Pocket (the phone version) or on anyway. A phone opens Pocket unless the person chose the studio (pocketMode.ts). It shows each time until "Don't show this again" is ticked. |
| [`PerfBadge.tsx`](../src/components/PerfBadge.tsx) | The performance badge in the header: how smoothly playback is going (perfMonitor.ts), with Clear memory, and a warning with tips while playback lags. |
| [`PianoPanel.tsx`](../src/components/PianoPanel.tsx) | The on-screen piano: the computer keyboard's piano keys drawn as a keyboard, each with the letter that plays it, lit while played (from the keyboard, a MIDI keyboard or a click). Its octave buttons are Z and X. With a piano roll open, **Note entry** writes each key played into it at a cursor that moves on (PianoRoll.tsx), so a melody can be typed in rather than placed note by note with the mouse. State in pianoPanel.ts; the playing itself in liveInput.ts. |
| [`Popover.tsx`](../src/components/Popover.tsx) | A small panel dropped below the control that opened it, kept on screen and inside any clipping box, closed by Esc or a click elsewhere. The base of most of the app's popovers. |
| [`ProjectDrop.tsx`](../src/components/ProjectDrop.tsx) | Drop a .fledgetone.json project file anywhere on the page to open it (asking first when there's work on the timeline). |
| [`ReportProblemDialog.tsx`](../src/components/ReportProblemDialog.tsx) | Tell Two Birds Workshop something went wrong: a description, an optional reply address and, if the person agrees, technical details (shown in full before sending). It goes by the person's own email program, or they can copy it, or use the contact form on the website. |
| [`SearchPalette.tsx`](../src/components/SearchPalette.tsx) | Search everything (Ctrl+K, or the SEARCH button): tools, settings, instruments, starters and the guide. Enter runs the highlighted result: it opens the thing or takes you to the control and rings it. Shift+Enter on an instrument puts it on the selected track instead of adding a track. |
| [`SharedLinkOpener.tsx`](../src/components/SharedLinkOpener.tsx) | Opens a song shared as a link (#s=... in the address, see shareLink.ts), on page load or when one is pasted into an open page, asking first if there's work on the timeline. Renders nothing. |
| [`TempoControls.tsx`](../src/components/TempoControls.tsx) | Tempo controls: the header's typed tempo field, Fit to time (set the tempo that makes a stretch of the song last a given time) and the tempo finder (tempos that land the hit points on the beat, see tempoFinder.ts). |
| [`UndoableRange.tsx`](../src/components/UndoableRange.tsx) | A range slider whose adjustments are one undo step each (a drag, a burst of arrow keys, a double-click reset), used for most of the app's sliders. |
| [`UpdateNotice.tsx`](../src/components/UpdateNotice.tsx) | "Version 2026.10.xx is ready: Reload": a small notice in the corner once a new version of the app has downloaded in the background (pwa.ts). It waits while the song plays or an export renders, and the app never reloads by itself: Reload writes the autosave first, and What's new opens after it. Later hides the notice until the next time the app opens. |
| [`VersionsList.tsx`](../src/components/VersionsList.tsx) | The Versions list, in the studio's File › Versions dialog and in Pocket's Versions sheet: the versions of your songs this browser keeps (versions.ts), this song's first, each with when it was kept ("10 min ago", "yesterday 14:02"). Tap one to go back to it, after a confirm. |
| [`frameTicker.ts`](../src/components/frameTicker.ts) | One animation-frame loop for every readout that moves with the sound (the mixer's meters, the spectrum), each called at the rate it asks for. A loop of their own each meant forty callbacks a frame on a big song, every one writing to the page whether or not anything had changed, on the same main thread that schedules the notes. The loop runs only while something is listening. |
| [`keyboard.ts`](../src/components/keyboard.ts) | Shared rules for the app's global keyboard shortcuts (timeline, piano roll, guide). Shortcuts must never steal keys from something the user is typing into, but a slider or menu that merely has focus shouldn't switch them off either. |
| [`mySoundsFile.ts`](../src/components/mySoundsFile.ts) | My sounds as a file, to keep them safe or take them to another browser or computer: the saved sounds and starred instruments (mySounds.ts), with the recordings the sounds play (a Sampler's, a Drum Rack's...) inside it as a project file carries them. Opening one adds its sounds and stars to this browser's; a sound of the same name is replaced, as saving it again would. One track's sound can go in a file of its own too (Share this sound, "<name>.fledgetone-sound.json"), to send to someone: opening it adds it to My sounds and puts it on the track it's opened on. |
| [`offscreen.ts`](../src/components/offscreen.ts) | Rows and strips scrolled out of sight are skipped by the browser (content-visibility: hidden, set only once they're out of sight, so the rows on screen aren't clipped to their boxes; `auto` didn't save the drawing): not drawn, not laid out, and their meters not read. On a big song most of the timeline's tracks and the mixer's strips are out of sight, and every frame the page changed (the playhead's time, a meter) the browser went over all of them again: most of the page's time while a big song played. |
| [`useFloatingMenu.tsx`](../src/components/useFloatingMenu.tsx) | A hook for a panel floating beside a button (portalled to the page body, on whichever side has room), closed by a click elsewhere, Esc or scrolling. |

## src/components/game/

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`GameTryOut.tsx`](../src/components/game/GameTryOut.tsx) | Try it in a game: little games that play the song the way a real game would. Three to pick from: a 3D arena (a robot hero, a guard and coins: tryOutScene.ts), a 2D platformer (blobs, gaps and a flag: platformerScene.ts), both through the game kit's own web player, and a rhythm game whose notes are the song's own (RhythmTryOut.tsx). In the first two, exploring plays the calm state, an enemy spotting the hero switches to the fight state by the song's transition rule and turns the intensity up as it closes in, coins fire the item stinger and a coin sound, and winning (beating the guard, reaching the flag) or losing plays the win or lose stinger. A panel picks which state, stinger and sound each moment plays (guessed from their names: tryOut.ts). Sounds the song doesn't have come from the sound effects maker. |
| [`RhythmTryOut.tsx`](../src/components/game/RhythmTryOut.tsx) | Try it in a game, the rhythm game: the whole song is rendered as it exports, its notes become the chart (store/rhythmChart.ts) and they fall down four lanes to be hit in time (rhythmGame.ts). The difficulty thins or thickens the chart; the timing offset lines the notes up with what's heard on this computer (Bluetooth headphones, for one, play late). Both are remembered in this browser. |
| [`platformerScene.ts`](../src/components/game/platformerScene.ts) | The game preview's 2D platformer, drawn on a canvas: the robot hero runs and jumps through a side-scrolling level of grass, gaps, spikes and floating platforms, collecting coins, to the flag at the end. One-eyed blobs patrol the ground: one notices the hero when it comes close and chases it; touching one hurts, landing on it squashes it. Falling into a gap or onto spikes hurts too. Like the 3D scene (tryOutScene.ts) it only reports what happens (events); the preview turns them into music and sound effects. |
| [`rhythmGame.ts`](../src/components/game/rhythmGame.ts) | The game preview's rhythm game, drawn on a canvas: the song plays and its own notes (the chart from store/rhythmChart.ts) fall down four lanes; press a lane's key (D F J K, or the arrows) as a note reaches the line. Hits are judged Perfect, Great or Good by how close they are; a note let past is a miss, and a miss muffles the song for a moment, as rhythm games do. Long notes are held to their end for a bonus. The picture is timed by the audio clock (minus the output's delay, plus the player's own offset), so what's seen is what's heard. |
| [`tryOutScene.ts`](../src/components/game/tryOutScene.ts) | The game preview's little game, in three.js: the hero (a small robot) walks a grassy arena collecting coins while the guard (a one-eyed cube) patrols. The guard notices the hero when it comes close and chases it; touching the guard hurts, but landing on it from a jump beats it. The scene only reports what happens (events); the preview turns them into music and sound effects. |

| File | What it is |
