## src/search/

The search palette (Ctrl+K) and instrument search.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`instrumentSearch.ts`](../src/search/instrumentSearch.ts) | Searching the instrument list: each instrument's searchable fields (name, its group's style and mood words, its description) and the ranked matches for what's typed, used by every instrument picker and the search palette. |
| [`paletteEntries.ts`](../src/search/paletteEntries.ts) | Everything the search palette (Ctrl+K) can find: the app's tools and settings, every instrument, the starters and the guide's sections. Running an entry does the thing (opens the Mixer, starts playback) or takes you to the control (scrolls to it, focuses it and rings it). An entry that can't be reached right now says why instead. |
| [`reveal.ts`](../src/search/reveal.ts) | Taking someone to a control: scroll it into view, focus it, and ring it for a moment so the eye finds it. Controls inside a panel that has to open first (the Inspector, a popover) may only appear a few frames later, so it waits for them (about a second at most). |
| [`searchCore.ts`](../src/search/searchCore.ts) | Matching typed words against things to find (instruments, settings, guide sections). Every word typed has to be found somewhere (so more words narrow the list), and where it's found decides the order: in the name beats in the keywords, which beats in the description. One slip of the fingers in a longer word is forgiven ("viloin" finds the violin), so is a missing space or hyphen between words ("8bit", "buildup"). |

## src/store/

The app's state and the music logic. timelineStore.ts holds the song and the actions that change it (with undo); timelineTypes.ts defines the data; project.ts saves and loads it. Most other files are pure functions on that data (markers, tempo, takes, notation, smart tools, starters...), unit-tested under Node.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`arrangeActions.ts`](../src/store/arrangeActions.ts) | The producer arrangement tools' store actions: write a dark melody, drop parts out or stop the beat before a drop, switch the beat (half time, double time or a new pattern) in a copy of a section, a riser or reverse cymbal into a drop, lay a loop out as a whole song (song form), and place the producer tag. Each is one undo step, and all of them only change clips, tracks and markers, so live playback and every export hear them the same. The maths is in darkMelody.ts, beatSwitch.ts, songForm.ts and producerTag.ts; this file applies it. |
| [`audioClips.ts`](../src/store/audioClips.ts) | Audio clip and Slicer maths with no audio or store in it, so Node can unit-test it: how a clip's length follows the tempo, what the edits do to its offset into the sound, which sounds a project uses, and reading these settings from a project file. |
| [`audioStore.ts`](../src/store/audioStore.ts) | Global audio-context state: running/suspended status, master volume and the audition-pad flash. Tempo and playback live in the timeline store. |
| [`autoFreeze.ts`](../src/store/autoFreeze.ts) | Auto-freeze: in a big song, the tracks nobody is working on are frozen by themselves in the background, so playback has room for more. It's the same freeze as the snowflake's (see freeze.ts), with three differences: the renders live in memory only (never in the project, the sound library or undo), they're made and swapped in only while the song is stopped (a render under way pauses while it plays, and nothing changes under a playing song), and a track is left alone until it has gone a few seconds without a change. |
| [`bass808.ts`](../src/store/bass808.ts) | The 808 designer's settings, stored on an 808 Bass track (Track.bass808) and saved with the project: drive and clip character with a tone control after it, the punch (a pitch drop at the start), slide time, decay, a top layer of harmonics small speakers can play, an output level, and an optional key the notes snap to. Absent, the track plays the original 808. The sound engine is src/audio/presets/bass808Designer.ts. Pure, so Node tests it. |
| [`bassTools.ts`](../src/store/bassTools.ts) | The heavy bass tools' settings and rules, apart from the 808 designer's own (bass808.ts): legato glide on monophonic synth tracks (Track.glide), the Sub enhancer (Track.subLayer: a clean sine under a bass's notes) and the Bass Drive insert (TrackFx.bassDrive: distortion on the mids and highs only, the sub kept clean and mono). Reading them from a project file, with defaults, so old files keep opening. Pure, so Node tests it. |
| [`beatSwitch.ts`](../src/store/beatSwitch.ts) | Beat switch and drop tools, on plain note lists: what each track is for in a beat (drums, bass, melody, FX), cutting a gap out of a part (a drop-out before a drop, or a stop: everything silent for the last beat or half beat of a bar), and the switch itself: a section's drums and bass in half time, double time, or a bass that follows a new drum pattern's kicks while the melody stays. Positions are bars from the start of the part (or section). No store or audio here, so Node can unit-test it (scripts/arrangeTools.test.mjs); arrangeActions.ts applies it. |
| [`bounceToPad.ts`](../src/store/bounceToPad.ts) | Bounce to pad, the plain maths: which Drum Rack pad a new sound goes on (the pad asked for, else the first empty pad of a Drum Rack track, else a new Drum Rack track), the rack with the sound on that pad, the level a bounce is stored at and the pad gain that plays it back as loud as it was, and the stretch of a recording an audio clip (a vocal take) plays, as a pad. No audio or store in it, so Node can unit-test it; the actions are in bounceToPadActions.ts. |
| [`bounceToPadActions.ts`](../src/store/bounceToPadActions.ts) | Bounce to pad: a stretch of the song (the whole mix, or one track as it sounds in it) rendered into a sound in the library and put on a Drum Rack pad, ready to play like any other hit; and a recording (a vocal take) put on a pad whole, or chopped at its hits onto the pads of a new Drum Rack. Each is one undo step, the new track included. Pocket and the studio both use these; the maths (which pad, the rack, the level) is in bounceToPad.ts. |
| [`breathe.ts`](../src/store/breathe.ts) | Let the music breathe: the tempo eases back into the end of every phrase and picks up again where the next one starts, as a pianist playing rubato does, written as tempo glides so the live song and every export follow it. The last phrase slows further, a small ritardando, and takes two measures to do it. |
| [`buildDrop.ts`](../src/store/buildDrop.ts) | "Build-up & drop here": the parts a drop is usually made of, written in one go before a bar. A riser and a noise sweep over the build with a reverse crash into the drop, a snare roll that speeds up over the build, and an impact with a sub drop on the drop's downbeat. |
| [`builtinPlugins.ts`](../src/store/builtinPlugins.ts) | Adding the built-in plugins (audio/plugins/builtinHost.ts) to the song, and the favourites and recently used ones the plugin browser (PluginBrowser.tsx) and the Plugins menu show. |
| [`busPresets.ts`](../src/store/busPresets.ts) | Bus presets: one-click group-bus setups, the inserts a mix engineer reaches for on each kind of group, made from the effects a bus already has (see buses.ts and TrackFx): - Drum bus: glue compression and a little saturation, so the kit hits as one. - 808 / bass bus: the low end in the middle (Mono bass under 120 Hz), saturation for harmonics small speakers can play, gentle compression to even the notes. - Vocal bus: a low cut, a little less boxiness and more air (Pro EQ), compression, and a de-esser (the Multiband compressor squeezing only the "s" range, over 5.5 kHz). - Music bus: a low cut that leaves the bottom to the bass, a gentle dip in the mud, light glue. Each also says which tracks belong on it, by what they do (trackRole), for grouping them in one go. Pure: no store or audio, so Node tests it. |
| [`buses.ts`](../src/store/buses.ts) | Group buses: a bus is a track with no clips of its own (instrument 'bus') whose strip the tracks routed to it play through, so a group of tracks shares one fader, its inserts and its sends. A track's `output` names its bus; a bus can play into another bus, but never round into itself. |
| [`ccLanes.ts`](../src/store/ccLanes.ts) | A note clip's controller lanes (CC 0 to 119) move its track's settings, as a MIDI controller's knob would: the controller's number picks the setting, by the track's MIDI learn mappings, else the usual meaning of the common controllers (7 volume, 10 pan, 74 cutoff...). Over the song the clips' lanes become automation lanes of their tracks, played by the automation engine live and in exports. A track's own automation lane for the same setting wins. (Plugins also get the controller itself, as MIDI: see the scheduler.) |
| [`channelKit.ts`](../src/store/channelKit.ts) | The channel kit's plan: which bars of the song make each piece of a streamer's or video creator's kit (audio/channelKit.ts renders them). - The loops (Starting soon, Be right back, Ending) are the song's main section (its busiest and most important, as Cut to length scores them), at most 32 bars; Ending is the calmest other section long enough to loop (4 bars and 8 seconds at least) when the song has one. - The intro is the start of the main section, about 6 seconds in whole bars, faded out. - The outro is the song's last bars, about 10 seconds (8 at least), from a section's start or a 4-bar phrase into one, ringing out as the song ends. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`chordTools.ts`](../src/store/chordTools.ts) | The piano roll's chord and riff tools: chords by scale degree (I, ii, V… of the key, one click each, voiced near the last), a fuller arpeggiator (more patterns, over one to three octaves, shorter or longer notes) and a riff generator (a phrase in the key that follows the chords under it). Plain maths, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`costumes.ts`](../src/store/costumes.ts) | Costumes and state options: the game music's second tier. |
| [`cutToLength.ts`](../src/store/cutToLength.ts) | Cut to length: make a 15, 30 or 60-second version of a song (an ad, a trailer, a social clip) by dropping or repeating whole sections, the way an editor cuts music to picture. Sections are the stretches between markers (or 8-bar phrases in a song without any). The cut always ends with the song's own ending, keeps the sections in order, and prefers the busiest and most important parts (a drop or a chorus over an intro). The tempo can then be nudged a little so it lasts exactly the length asked. This file plans the cut; the store rebuilds the clips. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`darkMelody.ts`](../src/store/darkMelody.ts) | The dark melody generator: a short loop (1, 2 or 4 bars) for trap, drill, rage and phonk, in minor, harmonic minor or phrygian. It writes a motif (half a bar for a 1-bar loop, a bar otherwise), repeats it, and changes the end of the repeats: a middle ending that hangs on a tension note and a last one that comes home, so the loop answers itself and wraps cleanly. The half step above the root (the flat second) appears in every melody, as a neighbour of the root or as the note that falls back onto it. Rhythms leave space: weighted 16th steps per style, thinned by the density, with a breath before the motif repeats. Seeded, so the same choices and seed give the same melody. Pure, so it's unit tested (scripts/darkMelody.test.mjs). |
| [`demoSong.ts`](../src/store/demoSong.ts) | Default tracks, and the stock patterns offered by "Insert pattern" on an empty lane (among them a mellow neo-soul groove in C major, Fmaj9 - Em7 - Dm9 - G13). Steps are 16th notes: offset = step / 16 bars. |
| [`dialogue.ts`](../src/store/dialogue.ts) | Dip under dialogue: find where people talk in a video's own sound, then dip the music there, the way a film mixer rides the score under the lines. Speech is found by its level in the voice band (300 Hz to 3.4 kHz), against the quiet between lines, with short pauses bridged so the music doesn't bob up between words. The dip is written as volume automation, so it shows on the tracks, can be edited, and plays the same live and in every export. No browser or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`dragSounds.ts`](../src/store/dragSounds.ts) | Drag-and-drop payloads from the sound deck onto the timeline. The deck (the bottom panel's old Instruments tab) is retired, so nothing sets them any more; the lanes still read them. The instrument is encoded in the MIME type because dragover handlers can only see dataTransfer.types, not the data, and lanes need to know whether to accept the drop. |
| [`dropMoves.ts`](../src/store/dropMoves.ts) | The Drop pad's moves: where its effects are held over the song, read from the notes of the tracks playing the Drop Pad (a note on a row holds that row's effect for as long as it lasts, see DROP_ROWS and effects/dropFx.ts). Live, the scheduler plays those notes as it plays any track's; an export reads them here and runs the effects over its render (masterAfter.ts), so the two match. As live, a muted Drop track holds nothing, nor one left out by solo; notes hidden by a clip's trim don't play, the sustain pedal holds notes on, and a note that runs past its clip's end still lasts its length. No audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`drumDesign.ts`](../src/store/drumDesign.ts) | The Drum Designer's settings: a synthesized sound for each drum row of the Designed Kit, each one or two layers of a drum voice (kick, snare, clap, hat, rim, tom, shaker, bell) with its own knobs, plus the presets (named by sound) and the checks that repair a project file's settings. Stored on the track (Track.drumDesign); the sound is made by src/audio/drumSynth.ts and played by src/audio/presets/designedKit.ts. Plain data, no Web Audio, so Node can test it. |
| [`drumGroove.ts`](../src/store/drumGroove.ts) | Swing per drum row: a clip's groove (ClipGroove) can give each row (each note name: the hats, the ride) its own swing, a push or drag in time and a velocity, so the hats swing while the kick and snare stay straight; and the groove templates (straight, light swing, heavy swing, lazy, pushed) that set those per row in one pick. The clip schedule (scheduler.ts) plays them; this is the plain logic, so Node can test it. |
| [`duck.ts`](../src/store/duck.ts) | Ducking under a proxy track: mark a track as the game's dialogue or sound effects (a "proxy": its clips stand in for what the game will play) and every other track dips wherever it sounds, the way video editors duck music under a voiceover. The dip starts a moment before the proxy does (look-ahead, so the first syllable isn't masked), holds while it sounds, and comes back after; short gaps are bridged. The result is a gain curve (1 = full level) the engine plays on every other track, live and in exports, and it follows the proxy's clips as you edit them. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`duckToKick.ts`](../src/store/duckToKick.ts) | Duck everything to the kick: one click puts a kick-triggered Pump on every part that isn't drums, a voice or a sound effect (the bass, chords, pads and leads), so the whole song breathes with the kick the way dance music does. The bass ducks deepest and comes back quickest, out of the kick's way; the other parts dip less and swell back over about half a beat, which is the pumping you hear. Plain data in and out, so Node can test it; the store makes it one undo step. |
| [`editorMarkers.ts`](../src/store/editorMarkers.ts) | Markers for video editing software: the song's markers as files Premiere Pro (FCP 7 XML), DaVinci Resolve (an EDL of timeline markers), Final Cut Pro (FCPXML) and spreadsheets (CSV) import, so the editor sees the section names and hit points on their own timeline. No browser or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`expression.ts`](../src/store/expression.ts) | Expression: a note clip's controller lanes, as a MIDI keyboard's wheels and pedal would play them. - Pitch bend (semitones): every note on the track bends together, gliding between points. - Mod wheel (0 to 1): dynamics, from soft and dark to loud and bright, on every instrument. - Vibrato (0 to 1): as deep as the lane is up. - Sustain pedal (down or up): a note let go while the pedal is down rings on until it comes up. Before a lane's first point it rests (no bend, wheel down, pedal up). Pure, so it's unit tested (scripts/expression.test.mjs). |
| [`flipActions.ts`](../src/store/flipActions.ts) | The sample-flipping actions: chop a sample onto a Drum Rack's pads (with a starting pattern), a new idea for that pattern, matching the song to a sample or a sample to the song (its tempo and key), and the bass cut. Each is one undo step. The maths is in sampleFlip.ts, sampleAnalysis.ts and pitchShift.ts. |
| [`folders.ts`](../src/store/folders.ts) | Track folders: a group of tracks shown together under a folder row that names and colours them, folds them away, and mutes or solos them in one click. Each member carries the folder (so undo, saving and the autosave keep it with no more machinery), and a folder's members always sit together in the track list. No store or audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`freeze.ts`](../src/store/freeze.ts) | Freezing a track: its instrument, inserts and EQ are rendered once to a sound, and live playback plays that instead, so a frozen track costs about as much as one audio clip. |
| [`freezeActions.ts`](../src/store/freezeActions.ts) | Freezing, bouncing and unfreezing tracks: renders a track's instrument and inserts to a sound (see freeze.ts for how the live engine plays it), with progress. |
| [`gameParams.ts`](../src/store/gameParams.ts) | Game parameters: named numbers, 0 to 1, that the game sets as things change ("danger" as an enemy gets closer, "health", "depth" under water), each moving several things in the music at once: the intensity, a low-pass filter, the reverb, the music's volume, a stem group's level. The way FMOD and Wwise games drive their music, without the game knowing how it's mixed. |
| [`gameSfx.ts`](../src/store/gameSfx.ts) | The song's game sound effects: sounds from the sound effects maker kept with the project, so the game kit carries them next to the music (files with their variations, and a play call in every player). Kept as their settings, not audio, so a project stays small and a sound can be changed later. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`glueMix.ts`](../src/store/glueMix.ts) | Glue: a switch that makes a song's parts sound like one record instead of instruments playing side by side, the way a mix engineer ties a mix together. Switched on, it: - makes space (makeSpace.ts): each part loses the rumble under it, and parts in the lead's range give way to it; - puts the drums on a drum bus and the music parts on a music bus (busPresets.ts), each glued by gentle compression, the music bus breathing with the kick; - ducks the bass under the kick; - sends every part a little more to the shared reverb, so they sit in one room; - spreads the parts left in the middle a little apart (never the lead, the bass or the drums). Every change is recorded (GlueRecord: the value before and the value glue set), so switching it off puts back what it changed, but only where the value is still what glue set: a pan or an EQ changed by hand since stays. The buses it made go, and their tracks play to where the bus did. Plain data in and out, so Node can test it; the store keeps the record in MasterSettings.glueMix. |
| [`intensity.ts`](../src/store/intensity.ts) | Intensity: one number, 0 to 1, that a game turns up as things get exciting. Tracks belong to stem groups (Ambient, Percussion, Tension, Climax, or any name), and each group has a curve: how loud its tracks play (0 to 1) at each intensity. Turning the intensity up crossfades the groups in and out along their curves, the way an adaptive music system mixes layers. Tracks without a group always play at full level. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`keyChange.ts`](../src/store/keyChange.ts) | A key change: every pitched note from a bar onward moves by some semitones. Drum kits, percussion, sound effects, the FX track, the Slicer and audio clips keep their notes (their rows are sounds, not pitches). A clip that runs across the bar changes only from the bar on. |
| [`kickClash.ts`](../src/store/kickClash.ts) | Kick and 808 clashes: where the kick drum and a bass's notes hit at the same moment, the bass's low end piles onto the kick's and hides its punch. This finds those hits for one bass track (for the warning in the 808 designer), and gives the one-click fix: the track's Pump set to duck the bass under every kick, the standard sidechain trick. Pure, so Node tests it. |
| [`launcher.ts`](../src/store/launcher.ts) | The clip launcher: a grid of clips, a column per track and a row per scene, to play loops live and jam an arrangement together. Launching a slot plays its clip on its track over and over from the next bar line, in place of the track's arrangement; launching a scene launches its whole row. Stop the transport and the song plays its arrangement again. What was played can be written into the arrangement. |
| [`launcherView.ts`](../src/store/launcherView.ts) | The clip launcher (see launcher.ts) as the live engine hears it. While it's in use, each track it has taken over plays, from one bar to the next, either its arrangement, nothing, or one of its slots looping. Those stretches are the track's segments, in song bars: a launch lands on a bar line (the next one, while playing), so the segment it starts lies just ahead. |
| [`loopVariations.ts`](../src/store/loopVariations.ts) | Loop variations: a few takes of the same loop that a game can rotate through, so a player who stays in one place for twenty minutes doesn't hear the very same loop again and again. Every take keeps the loop's length, key and parts; what changes is the feel (each take gets its own Human drift, see human.ts, because its clips get new ids) and the drums at the turnaround: a snare fill, a tom fill, or the hats dropping out for the first half. Take A is the loop as written. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`makeSpace.ts`](../src/store/makeSpace.ts) | Make space: small EQ moves so the parts of a mix stop covering each other, the way a mix engineer carves room. From the notes each track plays (where they sound: a synth patch playing an octave down counts an octave down) it works out who does what (the bass, the lead melody, the parts supporting them) and then, on each track's parametric EQ: - every part above the bass loses the rumble under its lowest note (a low cut), so the bass owns the bottom; - parts reaching down into the bass's octaves are thinned a little there (a low shelf); - parts playing in the lead's range give way a little where the lead's presence is (a bell), so the melody comes through without being turned up. Only the bands it uses change, and only to make room: a band the user has already moved is left alone. Drums, sound effects, audio, buses and returns aren't touched. |
| [`markers.ts`](../src/store/markers.ts) | Marker maths: names, keeping a marker's bar and time in step with the tempo, the ripple edits, and reading markers from a project file. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`mathPatterns.ts`](../src/store/mathPatterns.ts) | Math patterns: music a formula writes. Generators make a clip's notes from a key (the right-click menu's Math patterns…), and tools reshape notes already there (the piano roll's TOOLS). Pure, so they're unit tested (scripts/mathPatterns.test.mjs). |
| [`melodyVariations.ts`](../src/store/melodyVariations.ts) | Variations on a melody, in its key: an answering phrase, the tune darker or brighter, simpler or busier, syncopated, moved up a step, mirrored, or a harmony a third above it. Everything moves by the scale's own steps (a "third" is a major or minor third as the key has it), so the result stays in key; notes outside the scale keep their sharp or flat. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`microVariations.ts`](../src/store/microVariations.ts) | Micro-variations: game sounds that play over and over (footsteps, weapon swings, UI clicks) need each play to sound a little different, or the ear hears a machine. From one short clip, make several takes, each with its own pitch, brightness, note length and loudness drawn at random within the bounds you set, so the game can pick one at random each time. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`midiLearn.ts`](../src/store/midiLearn.ts) | MIDI learn and automation writing. A knob or fader of a MIDI controller (its CC number) can be mapped to any setting a lane can drive (see automation.ts): moving it sets that setting over its whole range. With Write on, moves made while the song plays are written into the setting's lane at the playhead instead, replacing what the lane had there. |
| [`midiStore.ts`](../src/store/midiStore.ts) | MIDI input state for the MIDI popover: whether the browser gave the app its MIDI devices, which input is listened to, the last activity, and the computer keyboard piano. The choices are kept per browser (a MIDI keyboard belongs to the computer, not the project). |
| [`mySounds.ts`](../src/store/mySounds.ts) | The player's own picks, kept in this browser for every project: favourite instruments (starred in the instrument lists, listed first) and "my sounds" (a track's whole sound saved under a name: its instrument with its settings, synth patch, 808 or drum design, plugin and its knobs, inserts, EQ, sends, ring...). Picking a saved sound puts all of that on a track at once, so a sound set up once never has to be set up again. The level and pan stay the track's own (they're the mix, not the sound). Sampled sounds (Sampler, Slicer, Drum Rack, Multi Sampler) keep their recordings in the sound library; freeing unused sounds leaves those be (see mySoundIds). |
| [`notation.ts`](../src/store/notation.ts) | A note clip as sheet music: measures of notes and rests on a staff (or a grand staff), the way the notation view draws it and MusicXML exports it. Pure, so it's unit tested. |
| [`noteChance.ts`](../src/store/noteChance.ts) | Notes that don't play every time, as on a hardware step sequencer: a note's `chance` (75%, 50%, 25%...) and its condition (`cond`: play only on the 1st of every 2 passes, the 4th of every 4). A repeated section then changes a little each time round without writing it out again. |
| [`noteExpression.ts`](../src/store/noteExpression.ts) | Per-note expression (the way an MPE keyboard plays each key on its own): a note can bend away from its pitch and swell or fade with key pressure over its length. Pure maths, unit tested. |
| [`noteRepeat.ts`](../src/store/noteRepeat.ts) | Note repeat, for finger drumming: while a pad (or a key of the computer keyboard) is held, its drum plays again at a chosen rate, locked to the song's grid while it plays (to the tempo while stopped), and its velocity follows how hard the pad is pressed. The rates, the grid maths and the pressure curve, as plain functions; liveInput.ts and audio/noteRepeat.ts play them. |
| [`noteTools.ts`](../src/store/noteTools.ts) | The piano roll's composing helpers, on plain note lists: scales (which rows are in key, and pulling notes into it), chord stamps, and edits over a selection: quantize, humanize, strum, arpeggiate, legato, transpose. Positions are in bars from the clip start, as in NoteEvent. |
| [`partKind.ts`](../src/store/partKind.ts) | What part an instrument usually plays in a song, from its instrument alone (a new track has no notes yet): the drums, the bass, a pad or chords, a lead, or something else. A new track starts with the sends its kind of part is usually mixed with, and the piano rolls start a new note at the length its kind is usually drawn with. Plain data, so Node can test it. |
| [`patterns.ts`](../src/store/patterns.ts) | Linked clips ("patterns"): clips that share `pattern` play the same notes. Edit one and the others follow, wherever they sit on the timeline, as a pattern does in a pattern-based DAW. Each keeps its own place, length and track. What's shared: the notes, the controller lanes, the groove, the wobble rate and the step lanes. Plain logic, so Node can unit-test it; the store runs syncPatterns after every change (see timelineStore.ts). |
| [`penLength.ts`](../src/store/penLength.ts) | How long a new note is drawn, in both piano rolls (the studio's and Pocket's): the length last drawn, stretched or resized for that kind of part in this session, else the length its kind is usually drawn with (a 16th for drums, a quarter for pads and chords, an eighth for other notes, a bar for the FX instrument's risers). Kept for the session only, as the rolls' other choices are. |
| [`phraseDynamics.ts`](../src/store/phraseDynamics.ts) | Shape dynamics: a part's notes get louder and softer the way a player phrases a line, without drawing anything. The notes are split into phrases at each rest (a gap of an eighth of a bar or more, or every two bars of non-stop notes); within each, the loudness rises to the phrase's peak (its highest note) and falls away after it, higher notes leaning a little louder, and the phrase's last note eases off. Each phrase keeps its own average loudness, so the part's overall level, and any accents between phrases, stay as written. |
| [`pianoPanel.ts`](../src/store/pianoPanel.ts) | The on-screen piano (PianoPanel.tsx): whether it's open, and note entry, where each key played goes into the open piano roll at a cursor that then moves on (PianoRoll.tsx). Opening it turns the computer keyboard piano on (midiStore); closing it turns it back off, unless it was on before. |
| [`playheadClock.ts`](../src/store/playheadClock.ts) | The playhead as it moves, every animation frame while playing, for what has to move with it smoothly: the playhead line, the view following it, the editors' playheads, the reference video. |
| [`pluginEdits.ts`](../src/store/pluginEdits.ts) | Turning a built-in plugin's knobs as undoable edits (Fledge Synth's panel in the studio, its Sound tool in Pocket). The first move of a gesture makes an undo step holding the plugin's settings before it (checkpointPlugin in timelineStore.ts); moves of the same control close together, with nothing else done between, are the same step; choosing a preset is a step of its own. The new settings are read onto the track a moment later, so a save or a redo has them. |
| [`producerTag.ts`](../src/store/producerTag.ts) | The producer tag: a short recorded or imported sound (a voice saying the producer's name, say) kept in this browser for every project, placed at the start of a song or every few bars of a beat-store preview, with the beat ducked a little under it. The sound lives in the sound library (IndexedDB) like any other; which sound is the tag is remembered in localStorage. This file has the plain maths: where the tags go, trimming the silence around a recording, and reading the remembered tag back safely. No store or audio here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`project.ts`](../src/store/project.ts) | Project file format (.fledgetone.json) and browser autosave. Selection state is not saved; everything else needed to rebuild the arrangement is. Files and autosaves from before the rename (GrooveForge) still load. |
| [`recording.ts`](../src/store/recording.ts) | Recording MIDI takes: the settings, how a take gathers the notes it hears into a clip, and quantize. Pure, so the unit tests cover it; the live side (audio times, the Transport) is in src/audio/recorder.ts. |
| [`reopenLastSong.ts`](../src/store/reopenLastSong.ts) | At startup, the studio and Pocket both open the last song again by itself (a reload, or coming back the next day, carries on where you were), rather than an empty timeline with an offer to restore it: an offer that's easy to miss, and that a newer session would replace. |
| [`restoreVersion.ts`](../src/store/restoreVersion.ts) | Going back to a kept version (versions.ts): it opens as the song, and the song open until then is kept as a version first, so going back can itself be undone from the same list. |
| [`retroInstruments.ts`](../src/store/retroInstruments.ts) | Whether the instrument lists show the retro instruments (the 1990s General MIDI soundfonts, see instrumentCatalogRetro.ts). Off unless turned on, and remembered in this browser. Songs that use a retro instrument play it either way, and a track's own instrument is always listed. |
| [`reverseActions.ts`](../src/store/reverseActions.ts) | Play a block of music backwards, as a tape turned round: everything sounding from one bar to another (or one clip, through its track) is rendered to audio, reversed, and put back in its place on a new Audio track, and what it was rendered from is taken out of that stretch. Notes fade in and their reverb comes before them. One undo step brings the forward music back, and the new clip's Reverse button (in its audio editor) plays it forwards again as audio. |
| [`rhythmChart.ts`](../src/store/rhythmChart.ts) | The rhythm game's chart, made from the song itself: the notes falling down four lanes are the song's own kicks, snares and melody. The melody is the top note of whatever pitched parts play at each moment; its notes move across the lanes the way the tune moves (up a step: a lane to the right), kicks fall on the left and snares on the right. Strong notes (kicks, snares, notes on a beat) are kept first, then weaker ones fill in while there's room, so an easier chart keeps the song's backbone and a harder one adds the tune's quick notes. Long melody notes become holds. Plain data from store/showcase.ts, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`ripple.ts`](../src/store/ripple.ts) | Ripple edits (insert or delete bars across the whole song) as plain data, and the rules they move positions by. |
| [`sampleFlip.ts`](../src/store/sampleFlip.ts) | Flipping a sample: chopping it into up to 16 slices (at its transients, into equal parts, or where you put the markers), laying the chops on a Drum Rack's 16 pads, writing a starting pattern that plays them back in a new order on the beat grid ("Chop and play", seeded so the same idea always comes back the same), and the low cut that clears a sample's bass for an 808. Plain maths, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`sampleKits.ts`](../src/store/sampleKits.ts) | The Drum Rack's and the Multi Sampler's settings: defaults, reading them from a project file, and laying a Multi Sampler's sounds across the keyboard. Plain maths, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`samplePack.ts`](../src/store/samplePack.ts) | Sorting a sample pack (a folder of sound files, as it comes from a download) into what the app plays: drum one-shots into Drum Rack kits, pad by pad (kick, snare, clap, hats...); notes of one instrument (files named by their note, "Keys C3.wav") into a Multi Sampler each; loops and other one-shots as below. Read from the file names and the folders they're in, as packs name them. Plain logic, so Node can unit-test it; loading the files and making the tracks is samplePackImport.ts's. |
| [`sceneCuts.ts`](../src/store/sceneCuts.ts) | Scene-cut detection maths: how different two video frames look, and which of the differences along a video are cuts. A frame is a small picture (RGB bytes); two frames differ by their pixels and by their colour histograms, so both a camera move and a lighting change score low while a hard cut scores high. A cut must stand out from the frames around it, which keeps fast action from reading as a run of cuts. No browser or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`shareLink.ts`](../src/store/shareLink.ts) | A song inside a link: the project (without its sound files), packed tight, deflated and written in base64url after "#s=" on the app's own address. The part after # never reaches a server, so the song travels only in the link. Opening the link opens the song (see SharedLinkOpener). |
| [`showcase.ts`](../src/store/showcase.ts) | Showcase video: the notes the song plays, as the export draws them (audio/showcaseDraw.ts): each note's start and end in seconds from the start of the export, its pitch, its track's colour, and whether it's a drum hit (drums get a band of their own under the pitched parts). Only what's heard: muted tracks (and tracks muted through their bus or by a solo elsewhere) are left out, and a note hidden by a trimmed clip edge isn't shown. Plain data, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`slides.ts`](../src/store/slides.ts) | Pitch slides and dives on single notes, kept in the note's own bend curve (`expr.bend`, in semitones, see noteExpression.ts), so they need nothing new to save, link, copy or play: the scheduler plays a note's bend on a voice of its own where the instrument has them, else by bending the instrument as a whole (the mono basses, Analog Lead and Fledge Synth bend that way; Fledge Synth's bend range opens to 24 semitones for a wide one, see wamPlugin.ts). |
| [`smartActions.ts`](../src/store/smartActions.ts) | The store side of the writing helpers (smartTools.ts): each makes or changes one clip, as one undo step. |
| [`smartTools.ts`](../src/store/smartTools.ts) | Writing helpers that make parts from a few choices: chord progressions in the song's key (with smooth voice leading), chords that fit a melody, a bass line under chords, a drummer, and drum fills. All on plain note lists (positions in bars from the clip start), with no store or audio, so Node can unit-test them. Anything random is seeded, so the same choices give the same part. |
| [`songForm.ts`](../src/store/songForm.ts) | Song form: a whole song laid out from a 4- or 8-bar loop, the way a rap song is usually built: intro, hook, verse, hook, verse, bridge, hook, outro. Every section plays the loop over and over, with parts taken out or thinned so the song moves: the intro has no drums or bass, the verses a thinner beat (no hat rolls or open hats, the melody a little softer) so a voice has room, the bridge only the kick under the melody and bass, the hook everything, and the outro the melody alone. Optionally the drums drop out for the last half bar before each hook, so the hook lands. This file plans it; arrangeActions.ts builds the clips. Pure, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`songKey.ts`](../src/store/songKey.ts) | The song's key, worked out from its notes: how long each pitch class sounds, matched against the usual major and minor key profiles (Krumhansl-Kessler). Used to tune sound effects and stingers to the song. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`songVersions.ts`](../src/store/songVersions.ts) | Versions of a song for videos, streams and podcasts: the same mix with some parts left out. - Underscore: without the lead melody (and any voices), to sit under someone talking. - No drums: without the drums and percussion, for a calmer moment. The lead: the parts named "lead", else the loudest part playing one line at a time (the melody is what a mix puts on top), its pitch breaking near ties; an arpeggio, a pad, chords or stabs never count, so a song without a tune has no underscore. Only parts you hear count: a muted track stays muted in every version. Plain data in and out, so Node can test it; the export renders each version. |
| [`speedUp.ts`](../src/store/speedUp.ts) | Speed up into the drop: the tempo rises over the last part of a block of music (a share of it, in whole beats) and, by default, snaps back to the old tempo on the drop. Written as ordinary tempo points, so live playback, every export, the metronome, recording and the grid follow it, and Undo puts the old map back. Also the drum roll that can go with it (the snare or clap turning into 8ths, then 16ths, then 32nds) and where audio clips that follow the tempo are cut so each piece starts on its beat (each plays at the tempo where it starts). |
| [`speedUpActions.ts`](../src/store/speedUpActions.ts) | The "Speed up into the drop" store action: the tempo rises over the last part of a block and snaps back on the drop (or stays), with an optional drum roll that gets denser into it. One undo step that writes ordinary tempo points (and notes), so live playback, every export, the metronome, recording and the grid follow it. The maths is in speedUp.ts; this file applies it. |
| [`starterKit.ts`](../src/store/starterKit.ts) | The pieces genre starters are built from: tracks with their effects, clips of 16th-note steps, the master settings and the project around them. |
| [`starters.ts`](../src/store/starters.ts) | Song starters for the New dialog: a 16-bar arrangement in each style, with its tempo, a mixed set of tracks, sections marked, the loop on the whole song and the master set up for the style. Built from data, so they are ordinary projects once opened. Steps are 16th notes: offset = step / 16 bars. |
| [`startersLoudness.ts`](../src/store/startersLoudness.ts) | How loud each starter song plays: a loudness target for each group of starters, and the measured trim (in dB) that brings each starter to its group's target, so switching from one starter to another doesn't jump in level. createStarter applies the trim (trimMix) as the last step, after the recorded swaps, the swells and the glue. |
| [`startersWorld.ts`](../src/store/startersWorld.ts) | Two starters on the newer world recordings: a plaza groove on the Latin percussion with nylon guitar and trumpet, and a morning in the garden on mbira, balafon, folk harp, hand chimes and a didgeridoo drone. Every part plays a recorded instrument. |
| [`stepLanes.ts`](../src/store/stepLanes.ts) | Step lanes: rows of steps under a clip's notes, each set step holding a value (0 to 1, in the lane height automation uses) for one of the track's settings: a Fledge Synth macro or another of the instrument plugin's parameters by name, the Filter's cutoff, an insert's setting... A step not set holds the value before it. "Per note": the value changes at each note that starts in a set step instead of at the step's start, so the timbre changes with the notes. |
| [`stingers.ts`](../src/store/stingers.ts) | Stingers: short musical cues a game plays over its music when something happens (a win, a level up, an item found, game over), written in the song's key and played at its tempo, so they fit whatever is playing. Each kind has a little recipe; Variation changes its rhythm and register. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`swell.ts`](../src/store/swell.ts) | Swells: the mod wheel (dynamics, see expression.ts) drawn over notes as a player shapes a held line, so a phrase grows and fades instead of sitting at one loudness. Notes that touch or overlap make one phrase; each phrase gets its own shape, and the wheel elsewhere in the clip is kept. |
| [`synthPatch.ts`](../src/store/synthPatch.ts) | The Synth Designer's settings (a "patch"): two oscillators with unison, a sub and noise, a filter with its own envelope, an amp envelope, an LFO, drive and glide. Stored on the track (Track.synth) and saved with the project; the sound engine is src/audio/presets/designer.ts. |
| [`takes.ts`](../src/store/takes.ts) | Take folders and comping. Recording over the same span again (a loop's passes, or a punch over a take) keeps every take in one clip; the comp says which take plays in each stretch of it. - A MIDI take folder's notes are the comp's: each stretch plays the notes of its take that start in it. They're written into the clip's notes whenever the comp changes, so the clip plays and edits like any other (a comp change rewrites them from the takes). - A mic take folder plays the comp's pieces of each take's sound, cut where the comp changes with a short crossfade (expandAudioComp makes those pieces for the scheduler). Pure, so it's unit tested (scripts/takes.test.mjs). |
| [`tempoFinder.ts`](../src/store/tempoFinder.ts) | The tempo finder: given hit points in a video (moments that must land on the music, as seconds from bar 1), find the tempos that put the most of them on the beat. Film composers do this with a calculator; here it tries every tempo in a range, 0.01 BPM apart. No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`timelineStore.ts`](../src/store/timelineStore.ts) | The song and everything that changes it: one zustand store (useTimelineStore) holding the tracks, clips, tempo and meter maps, markers, loop, master settings and the view and transport state, with every action the UI calls, and undo. Plus the two bridges out of it: to the audio engine (connectTimelineToAudio) and to the browser autosave (connectAutosave). |
| [`timelineTypes.ts`](../src/store/timelineTypes.ts) | The project's data types (Track, Clip, NoteEvent, the insert settings, automation, markers, master settings and the rest) with their defaults, limits and small helpers (snapping, durations, frame grids). Everything the store, the engine and the project file share. |
| [`transitions.ts`](../src/store/transitions.ts) | Transitions into a game state: what plays as the music switches to it, the way adaptive game music smooths a change. A drum fill over the beat before the switch, a riser over the bar before it, or an impact on the new state's downbeat. Notes are given relative to the switch point in bars (a fill starts a quarter of a bar before it). No audio or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`tryOut.ts`](../src/store/tryOut.ts) | The game preview's wiring: which of the song's states, stingers and sound effects each moment of the little game plays (calm, fight, victory; a coin, a hit, a footstep), guessed from their names and kinds so a song usually works with no setup, and changed in the preview's panel. Also the enemy's distance-to-intensity rule. No audio, three.js or store here, so Node can unit-test it. |
| [`uiStore.ts`](../src/store/uiStore.ts) | Which dialogs, panels and dock tab are open, and the dock's height: kept in a store rather than the components, so the search palette and menus can open any of them. |
| [`versionPolicy.ts`](../src/store/versionPolicy.ts) | The rules for a song's kept versions (versions.ts keeps them): when the next one is due while editing, which old ones to thin out, and how a version's time reads in the list ("10 min ago", "yesterday 14:02"). Pure, so it's tested on its own. |
| [`versions.ts`](../src/store/versions.ts) | Earlier versions of your songs, kept in this browser (IndexedDB), so "go back to 10 minutes ago" is one tap. While you edit, autosave keeps one every couple of minutes (keepVersionWhileEditing); and the song open is kept just before something replaces it: New, Open, a shared link, or going back to a version (keepVersion). Old ones thin out (versionPolicy.ts). |
| [`videoStore.ts`](../src/store/videoStore.ts) | A reference video to score to (gameplay, a trailer, a cutscene): shown in a preview window that follows the playhead and as a lane of thumbnails under the ruler, and usable as the picture of a video export. It lives in this session only (a video is far too big for the autosave): the project keeps working without it. |
| [`vocalActions.ts`](../src/store/vocalActions.ts) | The rap vocal tools' store actions: put a vocal chain preset on a track, make an Ad-lib track ready to record, and double a take (rendered by vocalDouble.ts onto a new track under the take's, panned left and right and lower). Each is one undo step. The maths is in vocalChains.ts and vocalDouble.ts; this file only applies it. |
| [`vocalChains.ts`](../src/store/vocalChains.ts) | Rap vocal chain presets: one click puts a ready vocal chain on an audio track, made of the track's own inserts (EQ, Pro EQ, Compressor, Multiband, Bass Drive, Delay, Reverb...) with settings, named by how they sound. Applying one replaces that track's built-in inserts and nothing else (its volume, sends, plugins and clips stay); the Ad-lib chain also pans the track a little off centre, as ad-libs sit. Pure, so Node tests it (scripts/vocalChains.test.mjs). |
| [`warp.ts`](../src/store/warp.ts) | Warp markers: where moments of a recording land in the music. Plain maths (no audio), so Node can unit-test it and the player, the clip drawing and the editing all agree. |

## src/support/

Reporting a problem.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`problemReport.ts`](../src/support/problemReport.ts) | Reporting a problem to Two Birds Workshop: the address it goes to, and the technical details a report can carry (browser, audio, the size of the song, recent errors). The song itself is never included; the person can attach a saved project file if they want to. |

## src/tour/

The tour and tutorials' content and progress.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`lessons.ts`](../src/tour/lessons.ts) | The first-visit tour and the guided tutorials. A step points at a part of the screen (a CSS selector) and explains it. A step with a `task` waits for the person to do something and moves on by itself once they have, checked against the app's state. Each task can note how things stood when the step began (`begin`), so "add a track" means one more than there were. |
| [`tourStore.ts`](../src/tour/tourStore.ts) | Which tour or tutorial is running and at which step, and what this browser has done before: whether the welcome has been shown, and which lessons were finished (or where one was left). Kept in localStorage; if that's unavailable (private windows) everything still works, it just isn't remembered. |
